LESSONS.title: Why GPUs wait on memory
LESSONS.goal: An expensive GPU can spend much of a step waiting for data to arrive from memory, so an operation’s speed depends on the bytes it moves as well as its arithmetic.
LESSONS.recall: An external hard drive can hold a lot but copies files slowly. In your own words, what is the difference between how much it holds and how fast it moves data?
LESSONS.predict: An operation spends 8 ms fetching its data and 1 ms doing arithmetic. If the arithmetic became twice as fast, roughly how long would the operation take?
example: In DeepSeek’s production decode, each step adds roughly one token per running sequence, and every MoE layer has to read the weights of each expert that received tokens. What limits that step, and what did DeepSeek change?

Each expert sees only the tokens routed to it, often a handful per step. Every weight byte fetched from HBM then supports only a few multiply-adds, so the arithmetic units spend most of the step waiting for data. Faster tensor cores would leave that waiting time where it was.

DeepSeek stores routed-expert weights in MXFP4, four-bit values with one shared power-of-two scale per 32. That is a little over half a byte per weight instead of BF16’s two, so reading the same experts moves roughly a quarter of the bytes. The saving is real only because the kernels consume the format directly, without first expanding it back to BF16.

Decode also runs across 64–128 GPUs with expert parallelism. Each GPU then holds only a few experts, about 7 at EP64, so it reads fewer weight bytes per step, and each expert collects tokens from the whole group, so each byte read does more work. DeepSeek’s Q&A gives the drop in per-step memory traffic as the reason this raises throughput.

questions.prompt: Your team moves its chatbot to a GPU with twice the arithmetic throughput but the same memory bandwidth. Generating text for a single user barely speeds up. What is the most likely reason?
options: The faster units only help once weights are quantized
Each step mostly waits on reading weights from memory
The network streaming tokens back is the real limit
questions.why: Speeding up a resource that isn’t the limit leaves the limiting cost in place. A single user’s decode step reads every weight from memory and uses each byte for very little arithmetic, so memory bandwidth sets its pace.
questions.hint: In the reading's example an operation spends 8 ms fetching data and 1 ms on arithmetic. For a single user, which of those two would faster arithmetic units shrink?
option_feedback: Narrower formats can help, but faster arithmetic units speed up arithmetic in the current format as well. The issue is that arithmetic wasn’t taking the time.
Right. With one user, each step fetches all the weights to do only a little arithmetic with them. Doubling arithmetic speed leaves that transfer time where it was.
The network adds delay, but it would cap both GPUs equally regardless of the hardware swap. The lesson’s point is about what happens inside the GPU during each step.

questions.prompt: To speed up small-batch decode, a team stores expert weights in MXFP4 instead of BF16, cutting their size about fourfold. The step gets no faster. Profiling shows a kernel that expands the weights back to BF16 in memory before each multiply. Why didn’t the change help?
options: FP4 is too imprecise, so the GPU recomputes in BF16
Small-batch decode is compute-bound, so bytes don’t matter
Expert weights are too small a share of traffic to matter
The multiply still reads full-size BF16 weights
questions.why: A narrower format shortens a step only where bytes were the limit, and only if a kernel reads it directly. An extra pass that expands it back to BF16 in memory restores the full-size traffic, plus the cost of the pass.
questions.hint: A narrower format saves time only when the kernel consumes it directly. Follow the weights from storage to the multiply in this profile and see what size they are when the multiply reads them.
option_feedback: Precision can affect quality, but GPUs don’t automatically redo calculations because a format is narrow. The profile points at a different cost.

It is the other way round. With few tokens per expert, each weight byte supports very little arithmetic, so small-batch decode is limited by memory traffic, which is why the narrower format looked promising.
In a mixture-of-experts model, reading expert weights is a large part of a decode step, and each expert sees only the tokens routed to it. The weights matter. The way they were read is the problem.

Right. The narrow format saves bytes only if the matrix kernel consumes it directly. Expanding to BF16 first reads the FP4 data, writes a full-size copy and then reads that copy, so more bytes move than before.

questions.prompt: A blog post announces a new attention kernel that runs 30% faster than FlashMLA. Your manager asks whether switching would make your decode service 30% faster. What do you need to know before answering?
options: Attention’s share of a decode step at your batch and context
The new kernel’s MFU, to confirm it nears the hardware peak
Its prefill speedup, since decode uses the same kernel
questions.why: End-to-end gain is limited by the kernel’s share of the step. Attention is one kernel among many in a decode step, so a kernel speedup says little until you know how much of the step it takes at your batch size and context length.
questions.hint: In the reading, a FlashMLA kernel that was 5–10% faster changed end-to-end speed by at most 5%. What explained that gap, and what would you need to know to apply the same reasoning here?
option_feedback: Right. A kernel speeds up the whole step only by its share of the step’s time. DeepSeek’s internal kernel is 5–10% faster than the public FlashMLA, yet end-to-end performance differs by at most 5%.
MFU tells you how close a kernel gets to the hardware limit, but it doesn’t tell you how much of your step the kernel occupies. A perfect kernel that takes 10% of the step can save at most 10%.
Prefill and decode call different attention kernels in DeepInfer, and the question is about decode. Even the right kernel’s speedup needs its share of step time to mean anything end to end.

transfer: Your chatbot runs on a GPU that holds the model easily. A vendor offers a pricier GPU with twice the arithmetic speed but the same memory speed, and your manager expects answers to come out twice as fast. Explain why that might not happen.
Explains that the arithmetic units can only work on data that has arrived from memory, and moving it takes time
Says that if a step spends most of its time moving data, doubling arithmetic speed shortens it only a little
Suggests checking which cost dominates, or a fix aimed at data movement such as reusing fetched data or storing fewer bytes

The GPU can only do arithmetic on numbers that have already been moved from memory, and moving them is limited by memory speed, which the new GPU doesn’t improve. If each step spends, say, eight milliseconds fetching data and one millisecond calculating, doubling arithmetic speed saves half a millisecond and the step barely changes. Answers would only get much faster if arithmetic were the slow part. Before paying more, I’d measure where the time goes. If it’s data movement, grouping more requests so each fetch is reused, or storing numbers in fewer bytes, would help more.
LESSONS.takeaway: An operation takes as long as the slowest of moving its data, doing its arithmetic and coordinating its kernels, so speeding up the other costs does not shorten it.

activity.title: Choose which limit to investigate first.
activity.intro: For one toy operation, the amount of arithmetic divided by the arithmetic rate gives 2 milliseconds. Moving the needed data at the available bandwidth gives 8 milliseconds. Assume ideal overlap between the two. This is an estimate for one operation, not a measured whole-model latency.

fields.label: What is the ideal lower bound in milliseconds?
fields.why: With ideal overlap, the lower bound is the larger cost: max(2, 8) = 8 milliseconds.

fields.label: Which limit dominates this estimate?
options: compute
The arithmetic rate
memory
The rate at which data can move
fields.why: The data movement takes longer than the arithmetic under these assumptions. Faster arithmetic alone would leave the 8-millisecond limit.

fields.label: Which observation would best test whether that estimate describes a real run?
options: peak
Only the advertised peak arithmetic rate
trace
A runtime trace showing where time and data movement go
name
The name of the model
fields.why: A trace can expose actual waiting, transfers, and execution. The toy estimate is a hypothesis about the limiting resource, not evidence that a real run reaches that limit.

activity.conclusion: A simple estimate tells you what to ask the profiler. The observed execution should decide which change you try.

levels.1:
A GPU is a processor built to perform enormous numbers of arithmetic operations in parallel, which suits language models because they are mostly arithmetic. But the arithmetic units can only work on numbers that have already reached them. Model weights and working state live in memory, and during execution the data has to travel from there to the units doing the calculation, with some results traveling back, and that movement takes time.

So there are two different questions to ask about memory. Capacity is how much data fits, and bandwidth is how many bytes can move per second, and a model can fit comfortably and still run slowly because every step has to move a lot of data. The GPU’s large main memory is usually called HBM, short for high-bandwidth memory, while much smaller and much faster storage sits closer to the arithmetic units. A good deal of an engine developer’s work goes into arranging calculations so the data they need is already close by.

Picture an operation that needs eight milliseconds to fetch its data and one millisecond to do its arithmetic. Doubling the arithmetic speed leaves the eight-millisecond transfer exactly where it was, because data movement sets this operation’s pace. If the engine groups enough work together that the same fetched weights get used many times, each byte moved supports more arithmetic, and the arithmetic units stay busier until some other cost becomes the limit.

The work itself is carried out by kernels, the programs that run individual GPU operations, and many speedups come from better kernels that avoid writing an intermediate result out to slow memory, lay data out more efficiently or merge several small operations into one. Storing each number in fewer bytes helps too. That is one purpose of quantization, which represents values in a more limited format, though it raises its own questions about rounding, model quality and whether the hardware handles the format efficiently. For any optimization, what you want to know is which cost it removes and whether that cost dominates your workload.
levels.2:
Take one matrix product. A batch X[B,d] multiplied by a BF16 weight mapping d to h costs 2Bdh FLOPs and moves about 2(dh + Bd + Bh) bytes, the weight once plus the inputs and outputs. When B is much smaller than d and h the weight term dominates, so the arithmetic intensity, FLOPs per byte moved, comes out at about 2Bdh / 2dh = B. Compare that with the device’s ridge point, its compute rate divided by its bandwidth. NVIDIA’s H100 SXM datasheet lists 989 TFLOP/s of dense BF16 compute and 3.35 TB/s of HBM bandwidth, a ridge near 295 FLOPs per byte, so below roughly 295 tokens per step this product is limited by memory on that device.

That is why decode is cheap per token at moderate batch sizes. A step that must read 8 GB of weights at 3.35 TB/s cannot finish in less than 2.4 ms whether the batch holds one token or two hundred, so within that range a larger batch is almost free per token. Storing weights in FP8 halves the bytes, but FP8 compute is also twice as fast as BF16, so the ridge measured in tokens barely moves. Mixture-of-experts models complicate the count, because each expert sees only the tokens routed to it and so runs at a much smaller batch. DeepSeek’s Q&A about running DeepInfer in production gives this as a reason to spread decode across 64–128 GPUs. With the experts spread that widely, each GPU holds fewer of them, each expert collects a larger batch, and memory traffic per step falls. DeepInfer targets NVIDIA SM100 (Blackwell) GPUs and Huawei’s Ascend AI chips, whose figures differ from the H100’s, but the reasoning carries over.

Inside a GPU, data moves through a hierarchy of storage, from HBM to a shared L2 cache to the shared memory and registers of each streaming multiprocessor (the GPU’s individual processing cores), each level smaller and faster than the one before. A matrix kernel loads tiles of both operands into shared memory, reuses each tile many times from there and writes only the finished output. DeepInfer’s dense products go through DeepGEMM, DeepSeek’s library of matrix-multiplication kernels (bf16_gemm_nt and FP8 variants in layers/linear.py). Its FP8 path quantizes activations to E4M3 with one power-of-two scale per 32 channels (get_fp8_cast_params), a format that the tensor cores, the GPU’s dedicated matrix units, consume directly.

Kernel fusion, which merges several operations into one kernel, cuts the traffic between them. Run separately, normalization, rotary embedding, a rotation, an FP8 cast and a cache store would each read their input from HBM and write their output back. DeepInfer’s fused_norm_rope_hadamard_cast_store_kvcache in tilelang_ops/fused_transform.py does all five in one kernel and keeps the intermediates on chip, so the FLOP count is unchanged while four round trips through HBM and four kernel launches disappear.

Launch overhead matters most in decode, where each kernel does little work. The CPU spends microseconds enqueueing each launch and a step can contain hundreds, so DeepInfer records the whole sequence once as a CUDA graph and replays it with one call. Graphs are captured for fixed batch sizes in deepinfer/worker/cuda_graph_runner.py, where build_graph_batch_sizes produces 1, 2 and 4 and then every multiple of 8 up to the maximum, and select picks the smallest captured size that fits. Nine tokens therefore run as a 16-row graph with 7 rows (44%) of padding, while fifty-seven run as 64 with 11%. Finer intervals would waste less compute, but each extra graph costs memory and capture time.

The engine also guards the CPU side. execute_main_model in worker/model_runner.py runs inside forbid_cuda_sync(), which raises an error on any blocking CPU–GPU synchronization during launch. A single stray .item(), which copies one GPU value to the CPU, would make the CPU wait for the GPU to drain, and the asynchronous scheduler that overlaps CPU bookkeeping with GPU work would stop overlapping. tests/test_cuda_sync_guards.py enforces the rule.

Quantization saves bytes at some cost in precision, and the format decides how much. Block scaling with 32 elements per scale limits how far one outlier can distort its neighbors. DeepSeek’s Q&A lists MXFP4 (FP4 values with one power-of-two scale per 32) for routed expert weights, and an FP4 format with E4M3 scales per 16 values for the main KV cache. A narrower format shortens a step only where bytes were the limit, and only if a kernel consumes it directly instead of running a separate pass to expand it back to BF16.
levels.3:
The bound used above is the roofline model, which Samuel Williams, Andrew Waterman and David Patterson introduced in 2009. It says a kernel cannot run faster than the compute peak, or than bandwidth times arithmetic intensity, whichever is lower. Reiner Pope and colleagues at Google applied it to transformer inference in 2022, showing how batch size, sequence length and partitioning across chips move each operation between the two limits, and the Scaling Book’s roofline chapter and inference chapter, written by Google DeepMind researchers, give the most direct modern treatment. Both limits are ceilings, and real kernels fall short of them by amounts that depend on how they are written.

How far short is usually reported as model FLOPs utilization, MFU, from Aakanksha Chowdhery and colleagues’ 2022 PaLM paper, which divides the model’s necessary FLOPs per second by the hardware peak. Deciding what counts as necessary takes judgment. DeepInfer’s csrc/engine/flops_estimator.hpp weights each contraction by precision (FP4 as 1, FP8 as 2, BF16 as 4) to express work in FP8-equivalent FLOPs, excludes the draft model’s work, padding and replicated experts, and omits normalizations. Each choice is defensible and each moves the number, so two MFU figures are comparable only under the same conventions.

Measurements have shown how much of a model’s runtime goes to moving data. Andrei Ivanov and colleagues’ “Data Movement Is All You Need” (MLSys 2021) profiled BERT training and found that matrix multiplications accounted for nearly all the FLOPs but a much smaller share of the runtime, with the rest going to memory-bound element-wise operations and normalizations that fusion and better layouts could recover. Tri Dao and colleagues’ FlashAttention (2022) designed attention around that traffic, computing softmax piece by piece so exact attention could be tiled and the full score matrix never reached HBM. Later versions divided the work better and used the asynchronous copy engines and FP8 support of Hopper, NVIDIA’s previous GPU generation, and DeepSeek’s FlashMLA, which DeepInfer calls, adapts the idea to latent attention.

A faster kernel speeds up the whole step only by its share of the step’s time. DeepSeek’s Q&A about running DeepInfer in production gives an example. The public FlashMLA lacks one hand-tuned assembly optimization that makes DeepSeek’s internal decode kernel 5–10% faster, yet end-to-end performance differs by at most 5%, because attention is one kernel among many in a step. A reported kernel speedup says little about end-to-end speed unless it comes with the kernel’s share of step time at the target batch size and context length. Kan Zhu and colleagues’ NanoFlow (2024) works on the step instead of the kernel, splitting a batch into nano-batches so that compute-bound, memory-bound and network-bound operations overlap on one device, which raises utilization without making any single kernel faster.

How far to push fusion and low precision is still unsettled. At one extreme, “megakernels” fuse a whole forward pass into one persistent kernel to remove launch gaps entirely, and the Q&A says DeepSeek’s Mega MoE fused kernel beats unfused MoE at every expert-parallel and batch size within a scale-up domain, the group of GPUs joined by the fastest links. The price is portability, and DeepInfer maintains separate NVIDIA and Ascend paths. Evidence about low-precision formats holds only for the models tested, and perplexity on generic text often misses damage that shows up on reasoning or long-context tasks, which is why DeepInfer ships task evaluations in eval/ (the AIME math competition, GPQA graduate science questions and the HLE expert-level exam) alongside a perplexity reference in tests/models/offline_decode_ppl.json. A roofline also predicts real performance poorly once communication and scheduling interleave, so these trade-offs still have to be measured on the workloads users actually run.

LESSONS.title: Batching and overlapping CPU with GPU work
LESSONS.goal: How grouping requests into one model step saves work, and why a grouped request can still wait longer.
LESSONS.recall: Ten people send prompts to the same model in the same second. Which part of the work could the engine do once for all ten instead of ten separate times?
LESSONS.predict: In a batch fixed at the start, one user's one-line answer is done after 12 tokens while another user's report runs to 2,000. What happens to the first user's place in the batch for the next 1,988 steps?
example: A batch holds a short answer and a long answer, and the short one finishes first. What should the engine do with its place in the batch?
The finished request needs no more model steps. Its state can be released once nothing still reads it, and the long answer keeps its own separate state.
With a fixed batch, the short request’s place stays empty until the whole group finishes. Continuous batching instead admits a waiting request between steps and gives it fresh state of its own.

Reusing the place raises overall throughput. The newcomer still waited before it was admitted, though, and each step still takes time, so per-user delays have to be measured before anyone claims that each user got a faster answer.

questions.prompt: A server switches from fixed batches to continuous batching. Total tokens per second goes up, yet a few users say the first word of their answer now takes longer to appear. What explains both?
options: Requests in a shared batch now read each other's history, which slows attention
The CPU now does more scheduling work, so the GPU idles longer each step
Fuller steps do more total work but each takes longer, and newcomers wait for a free place
questions.why: Batching is judged on two numbers that can move in opposite directions: work completed per second and the wait each request sees. A fuller batch makes each step longer and can make a new request queue for a place, so throughput and one user's first-token wait can both rise.
questions.hint: Total tokens per second adds up every user's work at once. Follow one person who has just sent a request to the busier server instead: what could they be waiting for before their first word appears?
option_feedback: Tempting if batching sounds like mixing conversations, but each request keeps its own state. The engine shares weights and steps, never histories.
CPU idle time is a real cost, but it is a separate problem with its own fix (asynchronous execution), and it would lower total throughput, which went up here.
Yes. Keeping every place filled raises the work done per second, while a bigger step and a queue for places can lengthen one person's wait for the first token.

questions.prompt: With DeepInfer's zero-overhead scheduling on, a team halves the time of the GPU's decode forward pass, but decode steps barely get faster. What is the likeliest explanation?
options: The CPU's per-step work now takes longer than the GPU's, so the CPU sets the pace
Overlap adds the CPU and GPU times together, so halving one part barely shows
Decode steps are post-processed straight away, so they can't overlap
_correct_seqlens_qk makes the GPU wait for the CPU to send true lengths
questions.why: Under overlap the CPU schedules step N+1 and post-processes step N−1 while the GPU runs step N, so a step lasts as long as the slower lane. Speeding up the faster lane past that point buys nothing, and the CPU becomes the bottleneck.
questions.hint: With zero-overhead scheduling, the CPU's scheduling and post-processing run alongside the GPU's forward pass. When two jobs run side by side, the step can't end until the slower of them is done, so ask which one is slower now.
option_feedback: Yes. Overlap makes a step last as long as the slower lane. Once the GPU lane shrinks below the CPU's scheduling and post-processing, the CPU becomes the limit, which is why llm_engine.py has a TODO to strip per-request Python work from decode.
Adding the two describes running the stages in order. Overlap runs them side by side, so only the longer one counts.
It is prefill steps that are post-processed straight away. Decode steps are the ones saved in prev_step_state so their post-processing overlaps the next forward pass.
That function exists so the CPU never has to stop and wait. It repairs sequence lengths on the GPU from the previous step's accepted counts.

questions.prompt: A pull request deletes DeepInfer's DeferredRelease and returns each step's output objects to their pool right after the step, calling the delay wasteful. Its tests decode one request at a time. Which extra test would you ask for before approving?
options: A benchmark showing fewer allocations and lower memory use per step
Overlapped decode with early stops and preemption, checked against a run without overlap
The same single-request test rerun with asynchronous scheduling turned off
A check that every output tensor keeps the same shape and dtype as before
questions.why: Under overlap, step N's outputs are still being read while step N+1 runs, and DeferredRelease holds them until the next sampling sync point. A test only catches an early release if it runs overlapped steps where requests stop, get preempted or change rows, and compares the tokens against a run where nothing overlaps.
questions.hint: Under overlap, the CPU is still post-processing step N while the GPU runs step N+1. A one-request test never has an early stop or a preempted request, so it may never catch an object being reused while something still reads it.
option_feedback: That would confirm the saving the PR is after, but it cannot reveal whether a reader still held the memory when it was reused.
Yes. The risk is that step N+1 overwrites an object a consumer of step N is still reading, and that only happens with overlap on and rows changing hands between steps.
With overlap off, no step runs while the previous one is still being read, so this test cannot reach the bug the delay prevents.
A recycled buffer keeps its shape and dtype. The failure is wrong contents, which a shape check would pass.

transfer: A café takes orders one at a time and cooks each dish start to finish before starting the next. A friend suggests cooking several orders together and slotting in a new order whenever a dish is done, the way continuous batching works. In your own words, explain why that serves more customers per hour, and why one particular customer might still wait longer for their first plate.
Explains that grouping lets shared work serve several orders at once, like each weight read serving several requests
Explains that a finished order frees a place for a waiting one instead of leaving it idle
Recognizes that more total work per hour doesn't mean each person waits less, since fuller steps take longer and newcomers wait for a place

Cooking several orders together means the stove and the cook's setup serve many dishes at once, just as an engine reads each weight once for several requests. If a quick order finishes early, a waiting order takes its place right away instead of the burner sitting idle until the slowest dish is done. So the kitchen turns out more food per hour. But each round now has more on the stove and takes longer, and a new customer may wait until a place frees up, so someone who arrives at a busy moment can see their first plate later than before.
LESSONS.takeaway: Batching spreads the cost of each model step across several requests, and the scheduler decides which requests share each step and when they join.

levels.1:
Suppose ten people are using the same model at once. Their questions and histories differ, but every one of their requests runs through the same weights, so an engine can compute part of their work together instead of running each request from start to finish on its own.

That grouping, called batching, pays off because each weight read from memory now serves several requests. Many small matrix operations merge into a few large ones that keep the GPU’s arithmetic units busy, and fixed costs such as launching each GPU operation are spread over more useful work.

The requests still have separate lives, though. One person wants a one-line answer and another wants a long report, and if the engine fixes the group at the start and holds it until everyone is done, the short request’s place sits idle while the long one keeps generating. Continuous batching lets the group change between execution steps instead, so when a request finishes, a waiting one takes its place on the next step with fresh state of its own. The hardware stays busier, and no request ever sees another’s conversation.

Deciding what goes into each step is the job of the scheduler. It has to stay within memory limits while dividing every step among new prompts, long prompts and answers that are already streaming back to users.

The GPU can also sit idle for reasons that have nothing to do with the batch. Most of an engine’s coordination code runs on the CPU, which prepares each step, launches the GPU’s operations and processes what comes back, and if the GPU finishes a step and then waits while the CPU gets the next one ready, its arithmetic capacity goes unused. Engines close that gap by having the CPU prepare the parts of a later step that don’t depend on results still being computed while the GPU works on the current one, which they call asynchronous execution. The 2024 NanoFlow paper pushes the same idea inside the GPU, running compute, memory and network work at the same time so that no single resource waits on another.

None of this promises that any one request gets faster. A bigger batch takes longer per step and a new request may have to wait for a free place, so total tokens per second can rise while a particular user waits longer for the first word of their answer. That is why a scheduler is judged on two measurements, the useful work it completes per second and the waits that individual requests experience.
levels.2:
Batching helps decode most because of what one decode step has to read. Each request in a batch contributes one new position (more under speculative decoding, covered in a later lesson), yet the step reads every active weight from GPU memory once however many requests there are. The time that read takes, roughly the weight bytes divided by memory bandwidth, buys one token when one request is running and sixty-four tokens when sixty-four are. The batch can’t grow for free indefinitely, because the arithmetic grows with it and so does attention, which reads each request’s own KV cache. Once those catch up with the weight read, every extra request makes the step longer.

In DeepInfer the choice of who joins a step is made by a scheduler written in C++ (csrc/engine/scheduler.hpp), which the engine’s per-step function, LLMEngine.step, calls once per step. A request starts in the waiting queue, moves to prompted once its prefill is done and to running while it generates. Two settings bound each step, max_num_seqs on how many requests take part and max_num_batched_tokens on how many positions it computes. When a prompt is too long for the token budget that remains, _schedule_prefill runs only a piece of it now and leaves the rest for later steps, which is chunked prefill, and a helper called _adjust_chunk_size moves the cut so it never lands inside an image’s tokens.

Decode runs into a different limit. Every running request needs room for its next position in KV memory, which a block manager hands out in fixed-size blocks, and when _schedule_decode finds no free block it preempts a running request. Depending on the stop_preempted_request setting, that request either ends with status FINISHED_PREEMPTED or is reset and put back at the front of waiting to be recomputed from scratch. Requests producing structured output always stop, because their grammar state can’t be rebuilt.

In the default engine a step is either all prefill or all decode, and every data-parallel rank has to make the same choice, because all of them join the same expert-parallel communication inside the step (the parallelism lesson explains why). The scheduling function _schedule settles it with a vote, using an all-reduce, a collective operation that combines every rank’s preference. A rank with nothing to do still runs an empty placeholder step so that the group communication lines up.

The CPU’s share of each step is where asynchronous execution comes in. DeepSeek’s Q&A about running DeepInfer in production breaks decode step N into schedule(N) → forward(N) → sample(N) → post-process(N). Scheduling and post-processing are pure CPU work, and post-processing can’t start until the sampled tokens come back from the GPU, so when the stages run in order the GPU idles through post-process(N) and schedule(N+1). DeepInfer’s zero-overhead scheduling has the CPU schedule step N+1 and finish post-processing step N−1 while the GPU runs step N. A step then lasts as long as the slower of the two lanes, which in decode is normally the GPU’s forward pass and sampling. If the CPU’s work ever grew past the GPU’s, the CPU would set the pace, and that is why the engine’s main Python file, llm_engine.py, carries a TODO to remove per-request Python work from each decode step.

The overlap itself lives in Worker.execute_model_step in deepinfer/worker/worker.py, the function that runs one step on a GPU. It runs the forward pass for the current step, then post-processes the previous step, then samples the current one. For decode steps with DEEPINFER_ZERO_OVERHEAD_SCHEDULING turned on, it saves the current step’s state in prev_step_state so that its post-processing can overlap the next forward pass. Prefill steps are post-processed straight away.

The price is that the CPU schedules step N+1 before it knows what step N produced. When the engine drafts several tokens per step, the CPU doesn’t yet know how many were accepted, and so doesn’t know each sequence’s true length. A function called _correct_seqlens_qk repairs the lengths on the GPU, building a remap from each request in the new batch to its row in the previous one (−1 for newcomers) and adding the previous step’s num_accepted_tokens, so the CPU never has to stop and wait. Object lifetimes need the same care. The docstring of step warns that its outputs are released on the next call unless the caller clones them, and a DeferredRelease class holds each step’s metadata and outputs until the next sampling synchronization point, pre_sampler_sync, so nothing goes back to a pool while someone may still be reading it.
levels.3:
Once continuous batching became standard, the argument moved to how prefill, which is heavy on arithmetic, and decode, which needs little arithmetic but is sensitive to latency, should share hardware. Some systems, Sarathi-Serve among them, cut prompts into chunks and mix them into decode steps so a long prompt never stalls the streams already running. Others put the two phases on different machines, so they stop interfering and each pool can be sized for its own phase. DeepSeek’s production system takes the second route, and DeepSeek’s Q&A about running DeepInfer in production describes separate deployments for the vision encoder, prefill and decode. On a prefill machine the chunk size isn’t fixed. A fitted quadratic cost model, cost(q, c), predicts how long a step will take from the number of new tokens q and the length c of the prefix already computed, and the scheduler takes the largest chunk that fits the step’s time budget, up to 32,768 tokens. The open-source engine, when one engine does both jobs, alternates whole prefill and decode steps instead.

The same Q&A credits SGLang and NanoFlow as the prior work its CPU–GPU overlap follows. NanoFlow, from Kan Zhu, Baris Kasikci and colleagues in 2024, goes further than hiding CPU work. It splits a batch into nano-batches inside one GPU so that operations limited by arithmetic, by memory and by network all run at once. Its authors also push against the common assumption that serving is limited by memory, arguing that for most workloads it is limited by arithmetic and that engines lose throughput by running those different kinds of work one after another. They report up to 1.91× the throughput of the systems they compared against and estimate that NanoFlow reaches 50–72% of the best their hardware could deliver, measured on their own models and workloads.

Because a larger batch trades per-user speed for total throughput, scheduling claims are best compared as curves. The DeepInfer repository’s README plots decode output throughput against per-user speed, the tokens per second one user sees, measured on 64 SM100 GPUs, with each point a different number of concurrent requests. Running more requests moves a deployment along that curve toward more throughput and less speed per user, so a single tokens-per-second figure can come from nothing more than a bigger batch. A scheduler change helps only if it moves the whole curve outward, and a report that lets you check that gives time to first token and inter-token latency percentiles at the concurrency you plan to serve, along with how many requests were sampled.

Overlap brings its own class of bugs, in which data still in use is released or overwritten. DeepInfer’s DeferredRelease waits a full step before returning metadata and output objects to their pools, and cloned KV blocks are unpinned only after a CUDA event fires, a marker the GPU reaches once the copy has finished. A copy or a delayed free that looks wasteful may be what stops a later step from overwriting bytes an earlier consumer is still reading, so before deleting one an engineer has to find every reader of that buffer and the event that orders them. Early stops, cancellations, preemption with recompute and mixed sequence lengths all deserve tests, because each changes which request occupies a row between the step that was scheduled and the step that gets post-processed.

Some of this remains unsettled. Output lengths are unknown when a request is admitted, so every preemption policy is a guess about which request will finish soon, and recomputing a preempted request repeats its prefill. Speculative decoding complicates asynchronous scheduling too. In DeepInfer the CPU can fix only the total verification budget for step N+1, because step N’s confidence estimates haven’t come back yet, and a GPU kernel later divides that budget among requests. And the CPU’s work per step grows with the number of active requests, so at very large batches the coordinating CPU can become the bottleneck before the GPU does.

LESSONS.title: Paging the KV cache
LESSONS.goal: How an engine stores each request’s attention state, organizes that memory in blocks, and reuses state computed for an earlier request with the same beginning.
LESSONS.recall: A chat request is on its 500th generated token. Thinking back to the attention lesson, what does the KV cache spare the engine from redoing at this step, and what does it still have to compute?
LESSONS.predict: Two customers send the same 1,000-token system prompt, but one of them is served through a fine-tuned adapter. Should the second request reuse the first one's cached prefix?
example: Two requests have the same prompt token IDs. The second uses a different adapter that changes attention. Can it reuse the first request’s keys and values?
The first request’s keys and values came out of its base weights and its adapter. They are numerical results of that particular computation, so the prompt IDs alone do not determine them.

The second adapter can produce different attention state from the same IDs. Reusing the first request’s state would mix values from two different models without raising any error, because the tensors have the same shapes.

The fix is to put the model and adapter identity into the cache key, or to invalidate the affected state when the adapter changes. A test alternates the two adapters and compares cached results against uncached reference runs.

questions.prompt: A support bot sends the same 3,000-token set of instructions ahead of every user's question. After the team turns on paging, more requests fit in memory, but time to first token hardly changes. What would cut that time most directly?
options: Smaller pages, so less memory sits unused in each request's last block
Reserving each request's maximum length up front, so none waits for blocks
Prefix caching, so each request reuses the stored state for the shared instructions
questions.why: Paging and prefix caching remove different waste. Paging stops memory being reserved or stranded, which lets more requests fit, while prefix caching lets a request skip prefill for a beginning the engine has already processed, which is what shortens the first-token wait here.
questions.hint: Paging changes where each request's saved state sits in memory, which is why more requests fit. Before the first word appears, though, every request still has to process those same 3,000 instructions from scratch.
option_feedback: Smaller pages would pack memory a little tighter, which helps capacity again. The first-token wait comes from computing the 3,000 shared tokens, which paging never skips.
This is the contiguous scheme paging replaced. It wastes memory and still recomputes the shared instructions for every request.
Yes. Paging decides where state lives, and prefix caching avoids recomputing state that already exists. Here the cost is recomputing the same 3,000 tokens for every user.

questions.prompt: In DeepSeek's production system, a cached prefix of a few thousand tokens clearly beats recomputing it, but for a prefix of about 200 tokens the hit saves little or nothing. Why?
options: Recompute grows with prefix length, while lookup and fetch cost roughly a fixed amount
The GPU copy engine handles many small block copies poorly
Short prefixes only sit in the sliding-window slot, not the block cache
Short prefixes rarely produce a hit, so the engine recomputes them anyway
questions.why: A prefix hit travels a path of fixed-ish costs: a lookup that must finish before routing, a fetch into host memory, then a copy to the GPU. Recomputing a prefix scales with its length, so for a few hundred tokens it takes milliseconds, about what the round trip takes.
questions.hint: A hit has costs of its own: finding the cached prefix and fetching it. Recomputing costs work for every token. Only one of those grows as the prefix gets longer.
option_feedback: Yes. Recomputing costs work for every token, so it is tiny for a short prefix, while the hash lookup before routing and the trip from the storage cluster cost about the same either way.
That was a real problem, but DeepSeek moved the copy to GPUDirect RDMA because of it. It also doesn't explain why long prefixes are fine.
The sliding-window slot holds state for every request regardless of prefix length, and a 200-token prefix still has a full block in the block cache.
The situation is about hits that are found. A found hit can still save nothing if fetching it takes as long as recomputing.

questions.prompt: A team starts keying the prefix cache on token IDs alone, and the hit rate climbs from 40% to 55%. A week later, users of one fine-tuned adapter report odd answers on long shared prompts, yet the cache's lookup test still passes. What is that test most likely missing?
options: It never evicts blocks while a request is still active
It only uses prompts shorter than one block, so no hits occur
It doesn't time whether a hit beats recomputing
It checks that a hit was found, never that the reused values match an uncached run
questions.why: This is a content bug, where the right blocks are found but hold the wrong values. A lookup test passes in exactly that case because a wrong hit is still a hit, and the jump in hit rate is the bug showing up as reuse across adapters.
questions.hint: The cached keys and values depend on more than the token IDs; the adapter that processed them matters too. A test that only confirms a match was found can't tell whether the reused values are the ones this request would have computed.
option_feedback: Eviction during a live request is a real allocation bug to test, but here the right blocks are found. The trouble lies in what they contain.
If the test never produced a hit it would not keep passing on hit checks. And a prompt length at a block boundary tests allocation, not content.
Speed is a separate concern. A slow hit gives the right answer slowly, whereas these users are getting wrong answers.

Yes. Keys and values depend on the adapter as well as the token IDs, so the adapter belongs in the key. A test that alternates adapters over the same IDs and compares against an uncached reference would have failed.

transfer: Your company's chatbot puts the same 2,000-word set of instructions in front of every customer's question. Explain to a manager, in plain terms, how the engine can avoid doing the same work for those instructions over and over, and why a customer using a differently fine-tuned version of the bot can't share that saved work.
Explains that the engine can keep the state computed for the shared beginning and attach it to new requests instead of reprocessing it
Explains that reuse is only correct when the same model computation produced it, so a different adapter gives different saved values
Mentions a limit, such as the saved state taking memory or a lookup that can cost more than recomputing a short beginning

Every question starts with the same instructions, so the engine can process them once, keep the keys and values it computed, and attach that saved state to each new request. That is prefix caching, and it skips most of the work before the first word. A customer on a differently fine-tuned version can't borrow it, because their model computes different numbers from the same text, so reusing the first version's values would give wrong answers. The saved state also takes memory, and finding and fetching it isn't free, so for a short shared beginning it may not save much.
LESSONS.takeaway: A prefix-cache hit saves time only when the stored state was computed by the same model and adapter and can be fetched faster than it could be recomputed.

levels.1:
The KV cache you met in the attention lesson, the keys and values saved from every earlier position of a request, spares the engine from recomputing a request’s whole history at each generation step. Once many requests are served together, that saved state becomes the engine’s main memory problem, because each request’s cache keeps growing until it finishes, and new requests keep arriving that may begin with text the engine has already processed.

Suppose every request were given one contiguous stretch of memory. Nobody knows in advance how long an answer will run, so the engine would have to reserve room for the longest possible answer, and requests finishing at different times would leave holes of awkward sizes between the ones still running. Much of the memory would sit reserved or stranded instead of holding state.

Woosuk Kwon and colleagues fixed this in their 2023 PagedAttention paper, the work behind the vLLM engine, by borrowing paging from operating systems. The state is cut into fixed-size blocks, and each request keeps a table that maps its logical positions to whichever physical blocks happened to be free, much as an operating system maps a program’s virtual pages onto scattered physical memory. A request claims a new block only when its last one fills, and two requests that begin identically can point at the same blocks.

Once blocks can be shared, work can be shared too. If thousands of requests start with the same long system instructions, the engine can keep the keys and values computed for that common beginning, the prefix, and attach them to each new request instead of running the prefix through the model again. Engines call this prefix caching. The SGLang paper keeps saved prefixes in a tree, a design its authors call RadixAttention, so a request that shares only the first part of a beginning can still reuse that part.

Reuse is correct only when the match is exact in a particular sense. The text has to tokenize to the same IDs, and the model that processes those IDs has to perform the same computation, so a request served with a different adapter gets different keys and values from identical prompt text and cannot borrow the first request’s state.

A correct hit can still be a slow one. The saved prefix may live on another machine, and looking it up, transferring it and attaching it to the new request all take time, so for a short prefix recomputing it can be quicker. That is why a hit rate, which counts how often stored work was found, says nothing by itself about whether users waited less.

The memory all this takes grows with the amount of live context, which is the number of requests times their lengths, so in a conventional cache doubling both makes the stored state four times larger. DeepSeek’s models compress that state, as the next lesson explains, which changes the accounting without removing the pressure.
levels.2:
In a conventional cache each layer stores one key vector and one value vector per KV head for every token, so a token costs 2 × layers × KV_heads × head_dim × bytes_per_element bytes, and the whole cache is that times the number of live tokens across all requests. A model shaped like Llama 3 8B, with 32 layers and 8 KV heads of dimension 128 stored in BF16, needs 128 KiB per token, so 32 requests of 8,192 tokens each hold 32 GiB of cache before the engine has set aside any working memory. The number of KV heads is the term designers can change most easily. Llama shares its 8 KV heads among 32 query heads (grouped-query attention), and giving every query head its own would make the cache four times larger and every decode step read four times as many cache bytes.

DeepSeek V4.1 does not fit that formula, and DeepInfer’s cache allocator, deepinfer/worker/cache_engine.py, shows how far it departs. The main cache, ca_cache, has shape [num_blocks, block_size // ratio, 1, bytes_per_token] because several positions are folded together before anything is stored, and each stored entry is a latent vector from which keys and values are derived later. An entry takes 288 bytes in a 4-bit format with one scale per 16 values, or 528 bytes in MXFP8. Beside it sits an indexer cache, ica_cache, holding small 4-bit keys that sparse attention uses to decide which blocks are worth reading at all.

The sliding-window state is handled differently again. A sliding-window layer only looks at the most recent positions, so its memory never grows with context, and DeepInfer keeps it out of the pages entirely. Each request gets one fixed slot in swa_cache sized for window + DEEPINFER_MAX_BACKTRACKING_TOKENS positions, which by default is 128 + 6 = 134 per layer, the extra 6 letting speculative decoding back up after its 5 draft tokens are rejected. DeepSeek’s Q&A about running DeepInfer in production puts the stored size of that state at about 1.4 MB per sequence. Paged memory therefore grows with context length while slot memory grows with the number of concurrent requests, which is why get_num_state_slots sizes the slot pool from max_num_seqs (1.2 × max_num_seqs + 1).

The pages are handed out by a block manager written in C++, csrc/engine/block_manager.hpp. It keeps free blocks in a doubly linked list, reserves block 0 to mean "no block", and gives every block a reference count. allocate takes a free block and sets its count to 1, pin_block adds a reference when another sequence shares the block, and free puts a block back on the list only once its count reaches zero. Before any allocation, can_allocate_nolock answers OK, LATER when the request should wait for blocks to free up, or NEVER when it needs more blocks than exist and has to be rejected.

Forking a request shows how that sharing plays out. When fork_seq branches a new sequence off a computed prefix, the branch starts with a copy of the parent’s block table, so every full block stays shared. The partly filled last block is the exception, because the branch will write new positions into it and must not overwrite the parent’s, so when the branch is scheduled that block is copied into a fresh one, the pair is recorded in clone_blocks, and the request’s state slot is cloned as well. This is copy-on-write at block granularity, the same trick PagedAttention used to let several samples from one prompt share memory.

In DeepSeek’s production system a prefix hit travels a long path, and every leg costs time. The entrypoint first finds the hit by matching a hash chain over metadata, and because the hit length has to be known before the request is routed, that lookup adds directly to the request’s wait. A separate process then pulls the KV from a storage cluster into host shared memory, and a thread inside the engine copies it into GPU memory layer by layer while the forward pass runs. That last copy uses GPUDirect RDMA because the GPU’s own copy engine did poorly on many small block copies. Recomputing a prefix costs work for every token times every parameter, so for prefixes of thousands of tokens the fetch wins easily, while for a couple of hundred tokens recomputation takes only milliseconds and a fixed lookup and round trip of similar size can cancel the gain.
levels.3:
Kwon and colleagues reported that vLLM’s paging gave 2–4× the throughput of FasterTransformer and Orca at the same latency, with larger gains for longer sequences, larger models and decoding methods that share prefixes, such as beam search and parallel sampling. Earlier systems reserved contiguous space for each request’s maximum length, and when memory capacity is what caps the batch, every block reclaimed from that reservation becomes room for another request. The numbers are the authors’ own, on their workloads, but the mechanism carries over to any engine whose batch is memory-bound.

Where the cached state lives decides how requests should be routed, and here the systems disagree. SGLang keeps prefixes in GPU memory in its radix tree, evicts the least recently used ones first and has its scheduler favour requests whose prefixes are already cached, so it pays to send each request to the machine that holds its prefix. DeepSeek chose the opposite. Its block KV lives on a dedicated storage cluster running 3FS, DeepSeek’s distributed file system, and according to DeepSeek’s Q&A about running DeepInfer in production it is protected with 10+2 erasure coding, so a read goes out to 11 storage nodes at once and any 10 replies are enough to rebuild the data. Because any prefill machine can read any prefix, the router can ignore where a prefix was computed and balance on load alone, storage can be scaled separately from the GPUs, and a failed compute node loses no cache. Only the sliding-window state stays behind in the host memory of the machine that produced it.

Keeping state for days pays off only because reuse is long-tailed. DeepSeek expires prefixes after 3 days for agent traffic and 7 days for chatbot traffic, because in chatbot traffic a small amount of KV cache is read very many times, and the team reports that a 3-day lifetime would cost chatbot traffic 0.5–1% of its hit rate. These figures are author-reported, and the cache-management code is tied to DeepSeek’s internal infrastructure and is not in the open release.

DeepSeek’s mixed attention also limits how long a hit can be. The block cache sets the hit length in whole 128-token blocks, but the last block is usable only if the sliding-window state for it survived too, and otherwise the engine backs off one block and recomputes it. The Q&A states the overall cap as at most L − 134 tokens for an input of length L, the 128-token window plus 6 positions of speculative backtracking, and the next lesson explains the layer layout that makes this necessary.

Exact reuse is safe only when every input that shaped the cached numbers matches, which means the weights, adapter, tokenization, position encoding and storage format as well as the token IDs. A shared cache also leaks timing, since a hit returns faster than a miss and one user may infer that another recently sent the same prefix, so whether the cache is shared per user, per organization or globally is a security decision as well as a performance one.

Bugs here come in two kinds that need different tests. In an allocation bug a request gets the wrong blocks, which shows up with lengths just below, at and just above a block boundary, with eviction while a request is still active, and with forks from a partly filled block. In a content bug the right blocks hold the wrong values, which shows up only when cached runs are compared against uncached references, for instance by alternating two adapters over the same prompt IDs. A test that merely confirms the lookup succeeded passes in exactly the case where reuse is wrong, because a wrong hit is still a hit.

LESSONS.title: Compressed and sliding-window attention
LESSONS.goal: What changes when a model compresses its attention state, limits which positions each layer reads, shares state across layers, or rebuilds that state approximately.
LESSONS.recall: The last lesson said a token costs 2 × layers × KV heads × head size × bytes in a conventional cache. What does DeepSeek V4.1 store per position instead, and why does that break the formula?
LESSONS.predict: A model has 20 layers, and each layer lets a position look back only 128 tokens. Can a token 1,000 positions back still influence the next word it writes?
example: An engineer argues that because each layer attends over 128 tokens, replaying the last 128 raw tokens restores a 20-layer model’s state exactly. What is missing from the argument?
Take the first token in the replayed region. In the original run, its deeper representations absorbed information that reached it, layer by layer, from positions before the replay boundary.

A replay that starts at the boundary has no access to that upstream state, so it can compute a different deeper representation. The tensors keep their dimensions, but the information from before the boundary is gone.

Exactness needs its own test, comparing the replayed computation with the full reference on identical continuations, including boundary and long-context cases. If an approximation is acceptable, the tasks you intend to serve also need to be evaluated.

questions.prompt: A model uses a 128-token sliding window in every layer. A colleague says it therefore cannot use anything written more than 128 tokens ago. What is the best reply?
options: Agreed, since no layer can read further back than its window
Not quite, because recent positions already carry what lower layers read further back
Not quite, because paging keeps every older position available to those layers
Not quite, because the MLA latent vector summarizes the whole history
questions.why: A window limits what each layer reads directly, but layers stack. Position i in a higher layer reads positions whose representations already include information that lower layers gathered from older tokens, so the model's reach is longer than one window.
questions.hint: Layers are stacked, and lower layers have already pulled information from older positions into the recent ones. A higher layer reading its 128-token window is reading those enriched positions.
option_feedback: True of each layer's direct reads, but the positions a layer reads were themselves built by lower layers that looked further back.
Yes. Information can move up to a window's length per layer, so across many layers a recent position can depend on tokens far older than one window.
Paging decides where stored state sits in memory. It does not change which positions a windowed layer is allowed to attend to.
MLA changes what is stored per position. It doesn't give a windowed layer access to positions outside its window.

questions.prompt: A run with DEEPINFER_YOCO_PREFILL_TRUNCATION_MODE=compact gives slightly different log probabilities from the same run with the mode set to off. A teammate files it as a bug in compact. What is the likeliest explanation?
options: Compact drops query rows, so it should switch to mask, which matches off
The 140 kept tokens fall short of the 134 positions the window state needs
Replay reads only the kept suffix, which cuts the long path through earlier layers
questions.why: Mask and compact are two implementations of the same bounded replay, so they should agree with each other. Both differ from off by design, because a replayed window never rebuilds the older state that, through stacked layers, fed into it in the full run.
questions.hint: The reading describes off, mask and compact. Mask and compact are meant to agree with each other, but both cut something that off still computes.
option_feedback: Mask keeps every row but narrows the window the same way, so it computes the same function as compact and also differs from off.
140 covers the 128-token window plus 6 backtracking positions with room to spare. The default is chosen to be large enough.
Yes. With 20 layers of 128-token windows, exact window state depends on the last 2,560 tokens. Replay attends from max(s, i−127) only, so a small difference from off is expected.

questions.prompt: DeepInfer's level-2 YoCo check passes: mask and compact agree on log probabilities and top-K entries along a fixed trajectory. A product lead asks whether bounded replay is now safe to ship for long-document question answering. What evidence is still missing?
options: A rerun on more than 8 devices to cover larger deployments
The level-1 metadata check of visible keys and store slots
Confirmation that the checkpoint satisfies n_prefill_layer < n_layer
A comparison with truncation off, plus scores on long-context tasks
questions.why: Both levels of the check compare two implementations of truncation and never run off. Agreement shows the implementations are consistent, not that the approximation preserves quality, and DeepSeek publishes no task-quality numbers for replay.
questions.hint: The level-2 check compares mask with compact, two versions of the same truncation. Neither side runs with truncation off, so the check can't show what truncation itself costs on real tasks.
option_feedback: More devices would test the same two implementations against each other again. The comparison would still leave out the full computation.
Level 1 is the cheaper, narrower check, and it also only compares mask with compact.
The equivalence script already refuses a checkpoint that fails this, and passing it only shows the model has the layout replay assumes.

Yes. Both checked modes share the same approximation, so their agreement says nothing about its cost. Measuring that needs off as the reference and tasks whose answers depend on text before the replay boundary.

transfer: A colleague reads that a model uses a 128-token sliding window in every layer and concludes it can't use anything from earlier in a long contract. Separately, they hear that a replay shortcut 'agrees with another version of the shortcut', and conclude it's safe. Explain to them, in a few sentences, what each conclusion gets wrong.
Explains that stacked layers carry information from older positions into recent ones, so a window per layer doesn't mean older text is lost
Explains that two versions of an approximation agreeing doesn't show the approximation matches the full computation
Says what evidence would be needed instead, such as comparing against the full computation or checking tasks that depend on early text

Each layer only looks at the last 128 positions, but those positions aren't raw words. Lower layers have already pulled in information from older parts of the contract, so a higher layer reading recent positions is indirectly reading further back. On the second point, if two versions of the replay shortcut agree, that only shows they compute the same approximation. Both could lose the same older information. To know whether the shortcut is safe, you'd compare it against the full computation and test it on questions whose answers sit early in a long document.
LESSONS.takeaway: A smaller attention cache can come from storing a compressed representation, from limiting which positions each layer reads, or from an approximation, and only the approximation changes the model’s results.

levels.1:
So far the KV cache has meant a key and a value saved for every layer and every position. Nothing forces a model to store exactly that, and designers change both what gets stored and how later layers use it, so a memory shortcut that is correct for one architecture can be wrong for another even when both are called transformers.

One kind of change is to what gets stored. Multi-head latent attention (MLA), introduced in DeepSeek’s V2 paper, caches one compressed latent vector per position, and each layer derives its keys and values from that vector when it needs them. The saving comes from how the model represents attention information, so it is independent of paging, which only decides where allocated blocks sit in memory.

Other designs limit what a query can read directly. With sliding-window attention (SWA), a layer lets each position attend only to a recent stretch of the sequence, say the last 128 positions, which bounds both that layer’s attention work and the state it has to keep. Layers build on one another, though, and a recent position’s representation may already carry information that lower layers pulled in from much older positions. A 128-position window in every layer therefore does not mean the model has forgotten everything more than 128 tokens back.

Some architectures go further and let later layers reuse state that earlier layers produced. In the design Yutao Sun and colleagues called “You Only Cache Once” (YOCO) in 2024, one group of layers builds a single cache that all the remaining layers read. DeepInfer has its own producer and consumer layer paths for the DeepSeek model it serves, and that model’s configuration decides which layers play which role.

A shortcut can also give up exactness to save work. DeepSeek’s Q&A about running DeepInfer in production describes rebuilding a request’s sliding-window state by replaying only its most recent 128 tokens, with attention confined to that segment. DeepSeek calls the result approximate, because the replay never rebuilds the older state that fed into those tokens in the original run.

That can be a sensible trade as long as someone measures what it does to the tasks being served. Showing that two implementations of the shortcut agree with each other proves something narrower than showing that the shortcut matches the full computation.

When reading this part of DeepInfer, it helps to ask of each code path what it stores, what it reuses and what it recomputes. The answer tells you whether the path promises exact numbers or an approximation, and so which comparison would test it.
levels.2:
Stacked windows reach further than any single one. If every layer lets position i read the previous W positions, information can move W positions per layer, so after k layers position i can depend on tokens up to k × W back. DeepSeek’s Q&A about running DeepInfer in production applies this to V4.1, whose 20 decoder layers each use a 128-token window, and says that rebuilding their sliding-window state exactly would mean running the last 2,560 tokens through all 20 of them.

DeepInfer’s cache allocator, deepinfer/worker/cache_engine.py, keeps separate memory for each kind of state V4.1 needs. The paged block cache holds compressed latent entries of 528 bytes each in MXFP8, an 8-bit format with shared scales, and _kv_bytes_per_token checks that the latent width plus the width used for rotary position information (RoPE) matches that layout. Beside it sits an indexer cache of small 4-bit keys, which sparse attention uses to decide which blocks to read, and every sequence also gets a fixed state slot holding the sliding-window keys and values for the most recent 134 positions of each windowed layer.

Layer sharing follows the YOCO pattern. In DeepInfer’s YoCo runtime, v4_modules/yoco.py, the flag yoco_enabled is true when the configuration value n_prefill_layer is smaller than the total number of layers, and every layer from n_prefill_layer onward is a consumer. Consumer layers compute their block KV from a shared hidden state captured at the first consumer layer, so prefill only has to push the full prompt through the producer layers. The consumers still need sliding-window state of their own, and rebuilding it is where truncation comes in.

The setting DEEPINFER_YOCO_PREFILL_TRUNCATION_MODE picks how that rebuild runs. With off everything is computed. With mask every query row is kept but the window is narrowed so that keys before the kept suffix are invisible, while compact removes the truncated rows altogether, using yoco_boundary_compact to gather the kept positions and compact_yoco_boundary to rewrite cross-layer metadata that still described the old row layout. The kept suffix, DEEPINFER_YOCO_PREFILL_KEEP_TOKENS, has to cover the window plus the backtracking allowance for speculative decoding, which is why the documented default is 140 tokens against 128 + 6. Mask and compact compute the same function on different numbers of rows, so they should agree with each other, but both differ from off because both cut the long dependency path described above.

DeepSeek’s Q&A spells out the replay rule. When replaying from position s, the query at position i attends only to keys from max(s, i−127) through i. That makes the cost of a replay constant, whatever the context length or layer count, and it is also why the state it produces is approximate.

The prefix-cache hit policy combines these pieces. The block cache decides how long a hit is, and the sliding-window state decides only whether the last block must be recomputed. For an input of length L the hit can be at most L − 134 tokens, and the block cache returns some L1 below that cap, a multiple of 128. If window state is saved for the stretch from L1 − 128 to L1, the hit is L1. Otherwise the engine backs off one block and replays it. For a 10,000-token prompt the cap is 9,866, so L1 is 9,856. With window state present the engine computes the remaining 144 tokens, and without it the hit falls to 9,728 and the engine computes 272, where the first 128 only rebuild window state and the block KV for them is reused untouched.
levels.3:
Most of the evidence for these shortcuts is about cost. DeepSeek-V2 (2024), the paper that introduced MLA, reported a KV cache 93.3% smaller and up to 5.76 times the maximum generation throughput of DeepSeek’s earlier 67B dense model. Those figures compare two of DeepSeek’s own models, and V4.1’s attention differs in its details from V2’s, so they show what latent compression can buy in general and say little directly about V4.1.

The YOCO paper by Yutao Sun, Li Dong, Furu Wei and colleagues describes a self-decoder that produces one global cache for a cross-decoder to reuse, so that prefill can exit early without changing the output. That exactness holds because the model was trained with the sharing in place. DeepInfer’s bounded replay is a separate step added on top of a YOCO-style model, which shortens the consumer layers’ window rebuild and accepts an approximate result. DeepSeek’s Q&A about running DeepInfer in production says decoder replay nearly halves total prefill computation, but it gives no task-quality numbers for the approximation, so that claim covers cost only.

The equivalence checks in DeepInfer’s YoCo example README differ in how much they exercise. The level-1 check runs on one device in seconds without loading weights and compares the metadata that mask and compact produce, such as window pivots, visible keys and store slots. The level-2 check needs 8 devices and a compatible V4.1 checkpoint, feeds both modes the same fixed teacher-forcing trajectory, and compares log probabilities and top-K entries one by one, with every other DEEPINFER_* variable held equal. At both levels the comparison is between two implementations of truncation, and neither one runs off. Measuring the approximation itself would mean running off and compact on the same trajectories, reporting the log-probability gap by distance from the replay boundary, and then scoring long-context tasks whose answers depend on text well before that boundary.

These paths also assume a particular model. They depend on n_prefill_layer, on which layers use windows and on which layers share KV, and the equivalence script refuses any checkpoint that fails n_prefill_layer < n_layer. A fine-tune of V4.1 keeps that layout, while a different architecture does not, even when its configuration file looks similar.

It is still open whether a model should be trained with the serving approximation in place, which would make replay exact by construction, as YOCO’s layer sharing is. It is also open how much quality loss a replay scheme may cost and on which tasks, and the sources publish no such measurement for DeepInfer’s replay.
