LESSONS.title: Spreading experts across GPUs
LESSONS.goal: How several GPUs divide a model’s weights and work, what they send each other, and why the slowest one sets the pace for the group.
LESSONS.recall: A mixture-of-experts model has hundreds of billions of parameters, yet each token runs through only a few experts. What has to be stored somewhere, and how much of it does any one token use?
LESSONS.predict: Four GPUs each hold a quarter of a model's experts. If the router sends half of all tokens to experts on one of those GPUs, how long will the layer take compared with an even split?
example: DeepSeek decodes across 64 GPUs with expert parallelism. Each MoE layer ends with a combine step that every GPU has to join. What happens when some experts are far more popular than others, and what does DeepSeek do about it?

The combine cannot finish until every GPU has processed the tokens routed to its experts. A GPU holding a popular expert therefore sets the pace, and the others wait. Average load says little here, because the layer takes as long as its busiest GPU.

Which experts are popular shifts with traffic, so DeepSeek’s expert load balancer counts each expert’s tokens. In decode it keeps one spare expert slot per GPU, collects load over 1,000 steps and reassigns experts every 10,000 steps, placing extra copies of hot experts on other GPUs so their tokens can be split.

The balance is still imperfect. DeepSeek reports that for decode the busiest GPU’s MoE load is 1.090 times the mean, and that its load balancing overall reaches roughly 80% of a perfectly balanced offline benchmark. Adding GPUs without changing placement would not shorten a layer whose busiest GPU is the limit.

questions.prompt: A team serves an MoE model on 8 GPUs with expert parallelism, each GPU holding the same number of experts. Every step, the profiler shows 7 GPUs finishing the MoE layer early and waiting. Which change targets this most directly?
options: Give each GPU an equal number of experts
Add more distinct experts so the router has more to choose from
Store copies of the busiest experts on the idle GPUs
Add GPUs so each one holds fewer experts
questions.why: The layer can't finish until every GPU returns its results, so it runs at the pace of the busiest one. Redundant copies of popular experts split their tokens across devices without changing which learned functions the router picks.
questions.hint: The router decides which experts each token needs, and you can't change that without changing the model. What you can change is which GPUs hold those experts, including extra copies.
option_feedback: They already have that. Equal counts don't mean equal work, because the router decides how many tokens each expert gets.
That changes the model itself, and new experts could end up just as unevenly used. The router's existing preferences stay.
Yes. A copy gives a popular expert's tokens somewhere else to go, so the busy GPU sheds work. The router's choices among logical experts don't change.
If the popular experts still sit together, one GPU still gets most of the tokens and the others still wait, now in larger numbers.

questions.prompt: DeepSeek runs prefill on 2 to 8 expert-parallel ranks but decode on 64 to 128. A newcomer asks why decode doesn't use the small group too. What is the main reason?
options: Decode prompts are longer, so they need more GPUs for activation memory
A small group gives each expert only a handful of decode tokens, so steps are spent reading weights
Wide groups let decode skip the dispatch and combine steps
Decode relies on tensor parallelism, which needs large groups
questions.why: Each decode step carries about one new token per request, so experts are short of rows. With 8 ranks, a 256-expert model choosing 8 per token gets about 15 tokens per expert, and a 15-row matrix multiply spends its time reading weights. Going to 64 ranks raises that to about 120 and shrinks each rank's share of weights.
questions.hint: Each decode step brings only one new token per request. Split across the experts, how much work does each expert get, and what does a matrix multiply with only a few rows spend its time on?
option_feedback: Decode adds one position per request per step, so its activations are small. Long prompts are prefill's problem.
Yes. Spreading many more tokens across the group gives each expert more rows per step, and each rank reads fewer expert weights, cutting memory traffic.
Every expert-parallel group still dispatches tokens and combines results. A wider group actually adds ranks to that exchange.
DeepSeek's Q&A says tensor parallelism isn't used for now. Decode splits by experts with data-parallel attention.

questions.prompt: A cloud team reproduces Wide-EP decode with its GPUs spread across several machines and sees far smaller gains than DeepSeek's EP8-versus-EP64 chart. What should they check first?
options: Whether dispatch and combine now cross slower links between machines
Whether the router's learned correction bias was loaded
Whether the load balancer reshuffles experts often enough
Whether they used the same number of GPUs as DeepSeek
questions.why: Scaling charts depend on topology more than device count. DeepSeek's evidence comes from one model on one hardware generation inside one fast domain, so the first question for a different setup is how many bytes cross which links per step.
questions.hint: DeepSeek's chart comes from GPUs connected by fast links. Once an expert-parallel group spans several machines, the dispatch and combine traffic has to travel over something slower.
option_feedback: Yes. DeepSeek's published benchmarks ran inside one scale-up domain. Across machines, token traffic travels over slower RDMA links and grows with tokens × chosen experts × hidden size.
A missing bias would skew routing, which is worth checking, but it would hurt small and wide groups alike and would not erase the gain from going wide.
Placement matters, yet DeepSeek reshuffles decode only every 10,000 steps. Balance figures near 1.09 leave too little room to explain a large gap.
Matching the count is not enough. Where those GPUs sit, and which links the traffic crosses, matters more.

transfer: A team serves a mixture-of-experts model on four GPUs, each holding a quarter of the experts. Most user questions this week are about programming, and the router keeps sending tokens to experts that happen to live on one GPU. Explain in your own words why the whole system slows down, and one thing the team could do about it.
Explains that one GPU gets far more tokens than the others because of which experts the router picks
Explains that the layer finishes only when every GPU is done, so the others wait for the busiest one
Suggests storing extra copies of the popular experts on the less busy GPUs, or another way of spreading their tokens

Each GPU holds the same number of experts, but the router doesn't pick experts evenly. With so many programming questions, the experts it favors sit on one GPU, so that GPU receives far more tokens than the other three. The layer can't move on until every GPU has sent back its results, so the other three finish early and wait, and the system runs at the speed of the busiest one. The team could put extra copies of those popular experts on the idle GPUs so they share the load. That uses more memory, but it spreads the work.
LESSONS.takeaway: Adding GPUs speeds up a model only when the work is spread evenly across them and the communication between devices costs less than the time saved.

levels.1:
Once a model is too large or too busy for one GPU, the engine has to decide which device stores which weights and which device does which work, and every choice brings its own traffic between devices. The schemes are named after what they divide. Data parallelism hands different requests to different devices, tensor parallelism splits one large matrix multiplication across several devices, pipeline parallelism gives each device a different run of layers, and context parallelism splits the work on one long sequence.

A mixture-of-experts (MoE) model invites one more kind of split. Its feed-forward layers contain many smaller networks called experts, and a router picks a few of them for each token, so any one token touches only a small share of the weights even though all of them have to be stored somewhere. With expert parallelism (EP), different devices own different experts. Each token is sent to the devices that hold the experts it was routed to, and the results travel back to be combined.

Owning the same number of experts does not mean doing the same amount of work, though. Suppose four devices each hold a quarter of the experts, but the router keeps choosing experts that happen to live on one of them. That device receives far more tokens, and because the layer cannot finish until every device has returned its results, the other three finish early and wait. The whole group runs at the speed of its busiest member.

Engine developers therefore count how many tokens each expert receives and time each device separately. When one expert is popular, the engine can store extra copies of it on other devices so they share its tokens. DeepInfer’s expert containers keep logical experts, the learned functions the router chooses among, separate from physical placements, which include those redundant copies. A copy adds capacity, but it gives the router nothing new to choose.

Copies take memory, and moving them means shipping weights between devices. The links themselves differ too, since a fast connection inside one machine behaves very differently from a slower one between machines. Judging a multi-GPU result means knowing where the weights live and how much data crosses which link, and a device count on its own says neither.
levels.2:
DeepSeek splits its model mostly by experts. Tensor parallelism would have to sum partial results across devices inside every layer, using a collective operation called all-reduce, whereas expert parallelism moves tokens instead. After the router picks experts, a dispatch sends each token’s hidden vector to the ranks that own them, and a combine brings the weighted results back. DeepSeek’s Q&A about running DeepInfer in production pairs this with data-parallel attention, one data-parallel group per expert-parallel rank, so each rank runs attention only for its own requests and never copies their KV caches elsewhere, and all ranks then meet in the MoE layer. Prefill uses 2 to 8 expert-parallel ranks (EP2–8). Decode uses 64 to 128, which DeepSeek calls Wide-EP, and tensor and context parallelism are not used for now.

Decode goes wide because each decode step carries only one new token per request (a few more with speculative decoding), so experts are short of rows to work on. Take a model with 256 routed experts and 8 chosen per token, the routing shape DeepSeek-V3 used, running 60 sequences per rank. Eight ranks together hold 480 tokens per step, which spreads out to about 15 tokens per expert, and a matrix multiplication with 15 rows spends nearly all its time reading the expert’s weights while the arithmetic units sit idle. At 64 ranks the group holds eight times as many tokens, about 120 per expert, and each rank stores fewer experts, so it reads fewer weight bytes per step. That is what the Q&A means when it says Wide-EP cuts the memory traffic of the expert layers.

In the code, the expert containers in v4_modules/moe.py keep four counts apart. logical is n_routed_experts, the range the gate chooses from, and extra is the number of redundant copies. Their sum, physical, is the number of expert weight sets actually allocated and must divide evenly by ep_size, and local = physical / ep_size is how many of them one rank holds. A helper in the load-balancing package, resolve_num_extra_experts, rounds the extra count up until that division comes out exact. The gate itself, TopKGate, adds a learned correction bias (e_score_correction_bias, with a second one for image tokens) to the routing scores before choosing. That bias is part of the trained model, and it is how DeepSeek steered the router toward balance during training without adding an extra loss term.

The trained bias cannot follow the traffic of the day, so at run time the expert load balancer, ExpertLoadBalancer, counts tokens per physical expert at every step and keeps a logical_to_physical_map that lets a popular expert’s tokens be split among its copies. Every so many steps, the placement policy recomputes where experts go. Its stated objective for each layer is to minimize, summed over recent steps, the largest load on any rank, and it works greedily, taking experts in descending order of load and placing each where it raises that sum least. The new weights are then moved between GPUs over NVLink. DeepSeek’s Q&A gives the production settings. Prefill starts with 4 redundant experts per GPU, collects statistics over 100 steps and reshuffles every 1,000, while decode starts with 1 per GPU, uses a 1,000-step window and reshuffles every 10,000 steps.

DeepSeek reports the result as moe_lb, the slowest rank’s MoE load divided by the mean. The Q&A gives 1.074 for prefill on four expert-parallel and four data-parallel ranks, 1.045 for prefill on two of each, and 1.090 for decode. Because the combine waits for the slowest rank, the decode figure means every MoE layer runs about as long as a rank carrying 9% more than the average share. If MoE time grows in proportion to load, perfect balance could shave somewhat under a tenth off that phase, which bounds how much more effort on placement could buy.

The lockstep reaches beyond the MoE layer. Every data-parallel rank must run the same kind of step, because all of them join the same dispatch and combine, so the scheduler holds a vote on whether the next step is prefill or decode, and a rank with nothing to do runs an empty placeholder step instead of skipping ahead.
levels.3:
The evidence for Wide-EP comes from DeepSeek itself. DeepSeek’s Q&A about running DeepInfer in production shows an EP8-versus-EP64 decode chart produced with the repository’s offline benchmark script, and it says production load balancing reaches roughly 80% of a perfectly balanced offline benchmark. Nobody has reproduced these figures independently, and they come from one model on one hardware generation, with the published benchmarks run on SM100 GPUs inside one scale-up domain. The 80% is DeepSeek’s estimate of what imbalance and routing cost on its own traffic, and another model or traffic mix could land somewhere else.

A wide group also fails as a unit. DeepSeek’s Q&A explains that all the GPUs of an instance form one communication domain, so a single failed GPU makes the whole instance unusable, and on restart the platform sets the EP size to however many healthy GPUs it actually gets. Restarts take minutes, so DeepSeek relies on spare instances and on rerouting requests, not on fast recovery. Long requests pin a large group in place as well, which is why a decode engine that receives a shutdown notice gets one minute to finish before its unfinished requests and their KV caches are forwarded to other engines. Because the recommended decode setup is EP64 or wider, the smallest efficient deployment is around 64 prefill GPUs plus 64 decode GPUs, and wide expert parallelism only pays for an operator who can run that much hardware.

Moving experts can change numbers as well as speed. The file parallel_utils/userbuffer.py configures DeepEP, DeepSeek’s library for expert dispatch and combine, and it turns off DeepEP’s multiple-reduction mode when batch invariance is enabled together with periodic expert rearrangement. When a copy moves, the order in which partial results are summed can change, and floating-point sums in a different order can differ in the last bits, so an engine that promises the same output regardless of batch has to account for its own load balancer.

Where the devices sit matters more than how many there are. DeepSeek’s Q&A says its fused Mega MoE kernel is the general choice within a scale-up domain at any EP or batch size. Once a group crosses machines, dispatch and combine travel over slower RDMA links, and their traffic grows with the number of tokens times the experts chosen per token times the hidden size. Checking a scaling chart therefore comes down to knowing where the experts live, how many bytes cross which links per step, and which collective waits for whom.

Several problems stay open. Placement is computed from the last 100 to 1,000 steps of load, so it lags behind shifts in traffic, and reacting faster costs more weight shuffling. Speculative decoding multiplies the tokens per step and changes how they route. Image and text tokens route differently, which is why the gate carries two biases, so a mixed workload can be unbalanced in ways neither kind of traffic shows on its own. And a balance figure built on averages can hide the occasional step where one rank stalls all the others.

LESSONS.title: Speculative decoding and DSpark
LESSONS.goal: How a cheap drafter proposes several tokens for the main model to check in one pass, saving time while the main model still decides the output.
LESSONS.recall: When a model writes "The capital of France is", why can't it compute the word after "Paris" at the same moment as "Paris" itself?
LESSONS.predict: You double the draft length from 3 tokens to 6. Should you expect each round to accept twice as many tokens?
example: In DeepSeek’s production service the draft model proposes 5 tokens per request at every decode step. Should the target model verify all 5?

A draft token becomes part of the answer only if every token before it in the draft was accepted. Its chance of being kept is therefore the product of the acceptance chances up to that point, so the fourth or fifth position of an uncertain draft rarely survives, yet checking it costs as much as checking the first.

DSpark adds a confidence head that predicts how likely each draft token is to be accepted. The scheduler ranks draft tokens by expected acceptance and, using a profile of how the hardware’s throughput changes with verification work, verifies the prefix of each draft that gives the most useful tokens per second.

DeepSeek’s Q&A reports that this cuts the drafts verified per step from 5.00 to between 3.2 and 4.4, while the average accepted length barely moves, from 3.29 to 3.20. The estimated throughput change depends on load: −1.5% at 16 sequences per GPU, +5.4% at 60 and +11.0% at 96. These figures are estimates computed from benchmark data and were not measured in a live A/B test.

questions.prompt: Two speculative decoding implementations both use exact speculative sampling with the same target model and seed, yet they print different strings for one prompt. A reviewer says one of them must be buggy. What is the best response?
options: Agreed, since the target checks every token and should force the same text
Not necessarily, since exact sampling promises the target's distribution, not identical strings
Not necessarily, since different drafters give different output distributions
questions.why: Leviathan and colleagues' guarantee is about distributions. Each output is a sample from what the target alone would produce, so a single differing string isn't evidence of a bug, while a frequency mismatch over many samples would be.
questions.hint: Exact speculative sampling makes a promise about the probability of each possible output. Two runs, even with the same seed, can draw different strings from the same distribution.
option_feedback: The target checks tokens through a random acceptance rule, and different drafters lead to different random draws and corrections.
Yes. Two correct implementations can sample different texts. Comparing them takes many samples and a check that the output frequencies match.
Under exact speculative sampling the drafter affects speed only. Whatever it proposes, the output follows the target's distribution.

questions.prompt: A team notices its drafter proposes the word "the" far more often than the target model would. They worry the final text will be full of extra "the"s. Under exact speculative sampling, should they?
options: Yes, because the target only checks that "the" is plausible, not how often
No, because every drafted token is rejected and resampled from the target
Yes, unless they switch to greedy verification
No, because over-proposed tokens are kept only often enough to match the target
questions.why: Verification keeps a drafted token x with probability min(1, p(x)/q(x)). When the drafter over-proposes, some of those proposals are rejected and replaced from the target's leftover distribution, which brings the token's rate back to what the target alone would produce.
questions.hint: The acceptance rule keeps a drafted token with probability min(1, p/q). Here the drafter's q for "the" is larger than the target's p, so look at what that ratio does to how often "the" survives.
option_feedback: The acceptance rule compares the two probabilities directly, so how often the drafter proposes a token is exactly what it corrects for.
If every token were rejected, speculation would save nothing. Tokens the drafter under-proposes are always kept.
Greedy verification is the same rule applied to a target that puts all its weight on one token. Both versions keep the target's rates.
Yes. A drafted token is kept with probability min(1, p/q), so an over-proposed "the" is sometimes rejected, and its final frequency equals the target's.

questions.prompt: You serve an internal tool with about 16 sequences per GPU rank. Going by DeepSeek's estimates for confidence-based verification lengths, should you turn the feature on?
options: Probably not, since at low load extra verified positions are nearly free
Yes, since it raises the average accepted length at every load
Yes, since verifying fewer positions always lowers latency for one user
Probably not, since the confidence head is poorly calibrated at low load
questions.why: DeepSeek estimates −1.5% throughput at 16 sequences per rank, +5.4% at 60 and +11.0% at 96. With few requests the step is memory-bound and extra positions ride along almost free, while with many requests each verified position takes compute another request could use. These figures come from a throughput model, not a live A/B test.
questions.hint: With only 16 sequences per rank, most of a decode step goes to reading the weights. Ask whether checking one more draft position at that load would take time away from anyone.
option_feedback: Yes. At 16 sequences per rank a decode step is limited by reading weights, so trimming verification saves little and throws away tokens that would have been accepted. DeepSeek estimates −1.5% there.
DeepSeek found accepted length barely moves (3.29 against 3.20). The gain comes from spending less verification work, which only pays when work is scarce.
Fewer verified positions can mean fewer accepted tokens per round, which makes a lone user wait through more rounds.
Calibration is an open concern, but nothing in the estimates ties it to load. The pattern follows from what limits the step.

transfer: A friend builds a speculative decoding demo where a small drafter guesses six tokens at a time for a large model. They're excited that it's much faster for them alone, and plan to use the same six-token drafts on a busy shared server. Explain why later guesses in a draft are worth less, and why the busy server could change the picture.
Explains that a later guess counts only if every earlier guess in the draft was accepted
Explains that checking guesses is nearly free for one user but takes work other requests could use on a busy server
Suggests measuring accepted tokens per round and speed at the expected load, or trying shorter drafts

The large model only keeps a guess if every guess before it was also kept, so the sixth token pays off only when the first five all survived, which is much rarer than any single guess surviving. For one user, checking those extra positions costs almost nothing, because the model spends most of each step reading its weights anyway. On a busy server that checking work competes with other people's requests, so wasted guesses slow everyone down. I'd measure how many tokens are accepted per round and the speed at real load, and try shorter drafts.
LESSONS.takeaway: Speculative decoding speeds up generation when the tokens the target accepts are worth more than the time spent drafting and verifying them.

levels.1:
In ordinary generation the model has to pick the next token before it has the input for the prediction after that, so every token costs one full run of the model and the runs happen strictly one after another. For a single person waiting on an answer, the length of that chain of runs is what sets the speed.

Speculative decoding, which Yaniv Leviathan, Matan Kalman and Yossi Matias described in a 2022 paper, gets more out of each run of the main model, which in this setting is called the target. A much cheaper drafter guesses several tokens ahead, and the target then scores all of the guessed positions in one pass, which costs little more than scoring one because the expensive part of a decode step is reading the weights.

The target keeps the guesses it agrees with and corrects the first one it rejects. Leviathan and colleagues gave an acceptance rule, usually called exact speculative sampling, under which the text that comes out follows the same probability distribution the target would have produced on its own. That is a statement about distributions, so two implementations given the same seed can still print different strings and both be correct.

Because a guessed token only counts if every guess before it was kept, the later positions in a draft are worth less than the early ones. If the drafter proposes three tokens, the third one helps only when the first two also survived, yet the target spends the same work checking it.

So the draft length is a bet. A long draft gives a request the chance to move several tokens in one round, but its tail is unlikely to survive, and when many users share the GPU the work spent checking that tail could have gone to someone else. DeepSeek’s DSpark paper makes the bet deliberately. It estimates how likely each prefix of a draft is to survive and weighs that against a measured profile of how its hardware’s throughput changes as verification work grows, and DeepInfer contains the scheduling path that turns those estimates into a verification length for each request.

When you evaluate speculation on your own model, the useful number is accepted tokens per target round set against the time spent drafting and checking, measured at the load you expect. A high acceptance rate on its own does not show a speedup, and a draft length that helps a lone user can waste capacity once the server is busy.
levels.2:
The cost of a long draft follows from how survival compounds. If each position survives with probability 0.8 given that the ones before it did, the second position survives 64% of the time and the fifth only about 33%, but the target pays the same to check the fifth as the first. On top of the accepted drafts the target always contributes one token of its own, either the correction at the first rejection or a bonus token after a draft that survives whole, so every round moves a request forward by at least one token.

What keeps the output faithful to the target is the acceptance rule. A drafted token x, which the drafter proposed with probability q(x), is kept with probability min(1, p(x)/q(x)), where p(x) is the target’s probability for it. Tokens the drafter proposes less often than the target would are always kept, and tokens it over-proposes are kept only often enough to bring them down to the target’s rate. When a draft token is rejected, the replacement is sampled from what is left of the target’s distribution after removing what the drafter already covered, max(0, p − q) renormalized, which fills in exactly the tokens the drafter under-proposed. Greedy verification, where a draft token is kept only if it is the target’s top choice, is the same rule applied to a target that puts all its probability on one token.

In DeepInfer this happens in Sampler._verification, in the sampler. Each row of logits is first mapped to its request and its position in the draft, and structured-output masks, which block tokens a required format forbids, are applied at every draft position. The sampler then compares the target’s log probability for each draft token with the drafter’s, which was saved during the previous round in a buffer called the MTP info pool, finds each request’s accepted prefix and packs the accepted and newly sampled tokens. After sampling, the draft head (DFlash in this code) runs on the new token to propose the next round’s drafts along with a confidence for each. A note in the sampler points out that this round’s verification reads what the previous round’s draft pass wrote to the pool, and that only the order of work on a single GPU stream keeps that read safe.

How many positions each request gets to verify is decided by the confidence scheduler. On the CPU, MtpVarlen::schedule collects every request’s survival estimates, sorts them from most to least likely, and adds them one at a time on top of the one token every request verifies anyway. At each total size it predicts the step time from a profile measured on the hardware for that graph size, and it keeps the size that gives the most expected tokens per millisecond. If request A’s estimates are 0.9, 0.8 and 0.6 and request B’s are 0.5, 0.2 and 0.1, three extra slots all go to A, and B verifies only its mandatory token. Under asynchronous scheduling the CPU plans step N+1 before step N’s confidences have come back, so it fixes only the total budget, and a GPU kernel in the confidence scheduler recomputes the survival products from the latest confidences and splits that budget among requests.
levels.3:
Leviathan and colleagues showed a 2–3× speedup on T5-XXL with identical outputs, using a small separate model as the drafter. DSpark, from Xin Cheng, Wenfeng Liang and colleagues at DeepSeek, changes both halves of the scheme. Parallel drafters that propose a whole block in one pass lose acceptance quickly toward the end of the block because each guess ignores the others, so DSpark adds a light sequential module that lets later draft tokens depend on earlier ones. It then schedules verification by confidence. The authors report that inside the DeepSeek-V4 serving system it speeds up per-user generation by 60 to 85 percent at matched throughput compared with their earlier production setup, which drafted a single token (MTP-1). The drafter, the traffic and the hardware are all DeepSeek’s own, so the figure describes their system against its predecessor.

DeepSeek’s Q&A about running DeepInfer in production separates out the scheduling half. Compared with always verifying all 5 drafted tokens, dynamic lengths verify between 3.24 and 4.44 per step while the average accepted length hardly changes, 3.29 against 3.20. The estimated throughput gain grows with load, from −1.5% at 16 sequences per rank to +5.4% at 60, which is near the production operating point, and +11.0% at 96. That pattern is what the roofline picture from the GPU lesson predicts. With few requests, a decode step is limited by reading weights from memory, so the extra verified positions ride along almost for free and trimming them only throws away accepted tokens, while with many requests each verified position takes compute that another request could have used. The Q&A says these figures were computed from EP64/DP64 benchmark data, so they come from a throughput model and not from a live A/B test.

The scheme only works as well as its confidence estimates. An overconfident head sends verification to tokens that will be rejected, which is why the verification path returns a batch_confidence_error that can be watched in production. The guarantee about the output distribution also holds only if draft and target probabilities are processed the same way at every position, with the same temperature, the same top-k or top-p cut and the same grammar mask, and a stop token that appears inside a draft has to end the sequence there. Speculation also gets in the way of determinism. The repository README asks you to turn variable-length verification off for deterministic sampling. It doesn’t give the reason, but a likely one is that the verification budget is shared across the batch, so how far one request gets verified depends on which other requests happen to be in the batch with it.

Several questions are still open. Nobody has a settled way to keep confidence estimates calibrated as traffic shifts between, say, code and prose, which are drafted with very different success. A drafter trained against a base model may be accepted less often once the target is fine-tuned, and draft length and batch size compete for the same step budget, so tuning one without the other can leave throughput on the table. A report on a speculative setup is most useful when it gives accepted tokens per round, drafting and verification time, inter-token latency percentiles and total throughput at the concurrency that will actually be served, broken down by kind of task.

LESSONS.title: Checking that outputs are right
LESSONS.goal: What different correctness claims about an engine change mean, and which comparison tests each one.
LESSONS.recall: Two runs of exact speculative sampling with the same seed print different sentences. What could still be true of both runs that would make them both correct?
LESSONS.predict: An engine with a JSON grammar returns valid JSON giving a company's founding year as 1897, when it was founded in 1902. Which part of the engine, if any, should have caught that?
example: A cache change produces valid JSON, but its next-token scores disagree with the reference at a page boundary. Should an exactness claim be accepted?
Valid JSON shows that the output followed a structural constraint. It says nothing about whether attention read the right positions or the right cached values.

The disagreement on identical prefixes contradicts the claimed numerical equivalence. The next step is to find the first position and layer where the values differ, starting near the page boundary where the error shows up.

The exactness claim should wait until that mismatch is fixed. If an approximation is acceptable instead, that is a different claim, and it needs a test of real task quality. Valid formatting is evidence for neither.

questions.prompt: You rewrite the code that reads the cache and claim the new path is exact. Afterwards the model still answers fluently and its JSON still parses. Which test would actually support your claim?
options: Generate long answers from both paths and check they read equally well
Run both outputs through the grammar and confirm every one parses
Feed both paths one fixed token sequence and compare scores at each position
Confirm the new path returns tensors of the same shape as before
questions.why: An exactness claim needs a trusted reference and a rule for agreement. Teacher forcing holds the inputs fixed so the two paths can be compared position by position within a stated tolerance, without diverging histories muddying later positions.
questions.hint: Fluent text, parsing JSON and the right tensor shapes are all true of a wrong answer too. You claimed the numbers are unchanged, so the test has to compare numbers on the same inputs.
option_feedback: Fluency is what you already have. A path that is slightly wrong can still write well, so this can't tell exact from close.
Parsing shows the format held. It knows nothing about whether the numbers behind each token were right.
Yes. With teacher forcing both paths see the same history, so any difference beyond rounding tolerance points to the first position where the rewrite went wrong.
An array can have the right dimensions and the wrong numbers, which is exactly the failure an exactness claim has to rule out.

questions.prompt: A user reports that one DeepInfer request, sent with the same seq_seed every time, gives different output at busy times than at quiet ones. Which cause and fix fit best?
options: The seed is shared across requests; give each request its own fresh seed
Busier batches change the order of sums; enable batch invariance as well
Prefix-cache hits skip sampling at busy times; turn off prefix caching
Grammar masks differ under load; remove the structured-output constraint
questions.why: The seed fixes the random draws, and batch invariance fixes the numbers those draws act on. Without it, a different batch can reorder floating-point sums enough to swap two nearly tied tokens, and from then on the whole continuation differs.
questions.hint: A seed fixes the random draws a sampler makes. At busy times, something else about how this request is run differs from quiet times, and the seed has no say over it.
option_feedback: A fresh random seed would make outputs vary even more. The seed is already fixed, and that is necessary but not enough.

Yes. A different batch can split sums into different tiles, changing the last bits and eventually a near-tied token. DEEPINFER_BATCH_INVARIANT=1 fixes the numbers, and the confidence scheduler also has to be off.
A prefix hit skips recomputing the prompt, not sampling. Generation still samples every new token.
The masks depend on the text generated so far, not on how busy the server is.

transfer: A teammate rewrites part of the engine and says it's fine because the answers still read well and every JSON output parses. Explain to them what those checks do and don't show, and describe a test that would actually support a claim that the rewrite is exact.
Explains that fluent text and parsing JSON show the format held, not that the model's numbers are unchanged
Proposes comparing the new path against a trusted one on the same fixed inputs, such as feeding both the same token sequence
Mentions that the comparison needs a stated tolerance or covers tricky cases like crossing a cache block boundary

Fluent answers and parsing JSON only show the output has the right shape. The grammar guarantees parsing no matter what numbers the model produced, and a wrong calculation can still read well. Since the claim is that the rewrite is exact, I'd compare it against the old, trusted code: feed both the same fixed sequence of tokens and compare their scores at every position, within a small rounding tolerance. I'd include cases that ordinary chats rarely hit, like a sequence that crosses a cache block boundary, because that is where this kind of bug tends to hide.
LESSONS.takeaway: Exact numbers, an exact output distribution, a valid format and an acceptable approximation are different correctness claims, and each needs its own reference and comparison rule.

activity.title: Check the numbers before judging a fluent answer.
activity.intro: Two paths receive the same fixed input IDs [1, 4]. The reference returns next-token scores [0.2, 0.8, -0.1]. A changed path returns [0.2, 0.805, -0.1]. Your stated rule permits an absolute difference of at most 0.001 in every score. Both paths still choose the second token when selecting the highest score.

fields.label: What is the largest absolute score difference?
fields.why: The second entry differs by 0.805 − 0.8 = 0.005. The other entries match.

fields.label: Does the changed path pass the stated numerical rule?
options: yes
Yes, because it chooses the same token
no
No, because one score difference exceeds the tolerance
fields.why: 0.005 is greater than 0.001. Matching the highest-scoring token does not establish that the numerical comparison passed.

activity.conclusion: A useful correctness check needs fixed inputs, a reference, a comparison rule and a boundary. Passing this one numerical case would still leave request isolation, stop behavior and task quality unchecked.

levels.1:
Suppose you change how a model reads its cache, and afterwards the program runs, the response sounds fluent and its JSON parses. None of that tells you whether the change preserved the model’s calculation, because an array can have the right dimensions and hold the wrong numbers, and a paragraph can read well while differing from what the reference model would have written.

Format is a good example of a property that is easy to confuse with correctness. Many applications ask for JSON, a text format that programs parse into named fields and values, and an engine can enforce it by giving the sampler a grammar that rules out any continuation the format forbids. The grammar guarantees that the answer parses. It has no way of knowing whether the date in a field is right or whether a fact was invented.

So testing a change starts with naming what it is supposed to preserve. A rewrite of the attention code that claims to be exact should reproduce a trusted implementation’s numbers within a stated rounding tolerance. A new sampling method that claims to be exact should leave the probability of each possible output unchanged, even if individual runs differ. A deliberate approximation is allowed to change the numbers, provided answer quality on real tasks stays within a limit agreed in advance.

Each of those comparisons needs a reference, usually a simpler implementation you already trust, and a rule for deciding whether the new path agrees with it. People sometimes call that check an oracle, though the name promises more than it delivers, since the check only knows about the property it compares.

The inputs also have to be held fixed. If two generators pick different tokens at some step, everything they see afterwards differs, and later disagreements tell you nothing. The usual remedy, called teacher forcing, feeds both implementations the same known continuation and compares their predictions position by position, so the first place where they disagree stands out and nothing after it is muddied by diverging histories.

Many bugs never show up in a pleasant example conversation. A cache bug may appear only when a sequence crosses a block boundary, a state leak may need two requests interleaved in a particular order, and a sampling bug may need a stop token to be proposed in the middle of a draft. Finding them takes test cases built to reach those situations.

Repeatability is its own question. A random seed fixes the draws a sampler makes, but a request can still come out differently when it shares a batch with other requests, because the grouping can change how the arithmetic is done. Keeping a request’s output the same whatever it is batched with is a separate promise, called batch invariance, and a seed does not provide it.

When you report a result, say which of these properties the evidence covers. A comparison of numbers on fixed inputs, for instance, says nothing about task quality or factual accuracy.
levels.2:
Most cases of the same input giving a different output trace back to floating-point addition, which gives different answers depending on the order you add things in. In FP32 the representable numbers near 10⁸ are 8 apart, so adding 1 to 10⁸ and then subtracting 10⁸ gives 0, while subtracting first and then adding 1 gives 1. A matrix multiplication or attention kernel sums thousands of products, and if a larger batch leads it to split that sum into different tiles, the last bits of the result change. Under greedy selection that is enough to swap two nearly tied tokens, and from then on the whole continuation follows a different history.

DeepInfer keeps batch invariance and deterministic sampling as separate settings. Setting DEEPINFER_BATCH_INVARIANT=1, which works on NVIDIA GPUs only, makes a request’s numbers independent of whatever else is in its batch. The runtime configuration file, worker/runtime_config.py, uses the flag to switch the kernel libraries DeepGEMM and TileKernels to deterministic algorithms and to tell the attention backend to do the same, and userbuffer.py turns off a multi-reduction mode in DeepEP, the expert-communication library, while experts are being rearranged. Deterministic sampling needs more on top of that, namely a fixed seq_seed in the request’s SamplingParams and the confidence scheduler turned off, since that scheduler varies how many draft tokens each request verifies. The seed fixes the random draws and batch invariance fixes the numbers those draws act on, so you need both to get the same output twice.

Teacher forcing is built into the sampler through a field called golden_output. Wherever an entry is not −1, the sampler emits that token instead of its own choice, which lets two implementations run over one fixed trajectory. DeepInfer’s YoCo equivalence check uses it to compare log probabilities and the top-K candidates at every position between two ways of truncating the prefill. The same page describes a cheaper first check that runs in seconds on one device without loading weights and compares only metadata, such as which keys each position can see and where they are stored. When the full comparison fails, the most useful thing it can report is the first position, and then the first layer, where the outputs part by more than the tolerance, because errors that begin at a cache-block boundary or at the replay boundary point to particular code.

Structured output runs through the same sampler. According to DeepSeek’s Q&A about running DeepInfer in production, each schema is compiled ahead of time on a dedicated machine into a grammar automaton, a state machine that tracks which text may legally come next, and the request picks up the compiled result before it enters the engine. During generation, Sampler._get_so_mask advances each constrained request’s matcher by the tokens accepted in the previous step and fills a bitmask over the vocabulary for the next position. When the engine is drafting several tokens at once, it also walks the matcher through each draft token, building a mask for every draft position until the grammar rejects one, and then calls matcher.rollback so that the grammar state again matches only the text that was committed. The masks are copied on a separate CUDA stream while the model computes its scores, and sampling waits for the copy to finish before applying them.

Failures in this path are kept to the request that caused them. If a matcher throws, the sampler marks only that request as FINISHED_SO_FAILED, because raising the error on the shared sampling path would take down every request in the step. A structured-output request that gets preempted for memory is stopped instead of being recomputed, since its grammar state cannot be replayed.

Each kind of change therefore comes with its own test. Turning on batch invariance should give bit-for-bit equal outputs across batch compositions. An exact kernel rewrite should match the reference elementwise, within a stated tolerance, along teacher-forced trajectories. A speculative sampler can legitimately produce different samples, so it needs a statistical test that its output distribution matches the target model’s. A grammar change needs every output checked by an independent parser, plus a deliberate search for tokens the mask wrongly allowed or blocked, especially tokens whose text straddles a boundary in the grammar.

LESSONS.title: From a fast engine to a usable service
LESSONS.goal: How queues, routing, state transfer and failure handling turn an engine into a service, and when running prefill and decode on separate machines is worth the handoff it creates.
LESSONS.recall: A user closes the browser tab halfway through a long answer. Which parts of the service around the engine have to notice, and what keeps running if none of them does?
LESSONS.predict: You split prefill and decode onto separate machines for a chatbot that gets two or three requests a second. Before reading on, guess whether its time to first token gets better or worse, and why.
example: DeepSeek keeps prompt caches for days on a dedicated storage cluster, so a returning conversation can skip most of its prefill. What does a hit cost on the way to the GPU, and which parts of that cost does the request actually wait for?

Before the request is routed, the entry point matches its prompt against the cache by walking a chain of hashes over token blocks. The hit length decides which machine gets the request, so this lookup cannot overlap with anything, and every request waits for it.

The matched cache blocks are then fetched from the storage cluster into host memory by a separate process, asynchronously. Copying them into GPU memory happens layer by layer while the forward pass runs, using network cards that write straight into memory so the copy takes no GPU compute.

DeepSeek put the cache on a shared storage cluster instead of each machine’s local memory, so any prefill machine can hit any prefix. Routing can then follow load alone, without sending requests to whichever machine happens to hold their prefix.

A hit still has to be judged by the time users see. If the fetch could not overlap with computation, a slow transfer could make a hit finish later than recomputing the prefix would. Reporting time to first token beside the hit rate shows which case the service is in.

questions.prompt: You move prompt processing to one machine and answer generation to another. Both machines are idle, yet the first test request now takes noticeably longer to start streaming than it did on a single machine. What new step is the likeliest cause?
options: Re-tokenizing the prompt on the decode machine before it can continue
Loading a fresh copy of the model weights for the incoming request
Sending the prompt’s attention state from the prefill machine to the decode machine
Holding the request in a queue until a decode slot becomes free
questions.why: Decode continues from the numerical state that prefill produced, so once the stages live on different machines that state has to cross the network before the first answer token can be generated. That transfer is the cost every split adds, and on a small, idle workload nothing offsets it.
questions.hint: Splitting the stages across two machines creates a handoff that a single machine never needed. Decode can’t start until it holds what prefill produced, so ask what now has to cross the network first.
option_feedback: The decode machine needs the computed attention state, and token IDs alone would force it to redo the prefill the split was meant to move elsewhere. A well-built split sends the state instead.
Weights are loaded once when a worker starts and then reused for every request, so they don’t explain a per-request delay.
Right. The attention state has to travel between machines, and that handoff adds to time to first token unless it overlaps with other work.
Queues add waiting when requests outnumber slots, but both machines are idle here, so nothing is ahead of this request.

questions.prompt: You put a small web server in front of DeepInfer’s LLMEngine. In a load test the client disconnects after the first few tokens of every answer, yet GPU memory and utilization stay high long after the test ends. What is the likeliest cause?
options: The server never calls abort_request when a connection closes, so those requests keep generating
The scheduler marks disconnected requests as aborted but never frees their cache blocks
Preemption keeps sending the disconnected requests back to the front of the waiting queue
max_num_seqs is set too high, so too many requests were admitted at once
questions.why: DeepInfer has no online-serving wrapper, so nothing inside the engine knows a client went away. Cancellation happens only when something calls LLMEngine.abort_request, after which the scheduler frees the request’s blocks and slot on its next pass.
questions.hint: DeepInfer’s engine docstring says the release has no online-serving wrapper. When a client hangs up mid-answer, which piece of code would have to tell the engine to stop, and does yours?
option_feedback: Right. The engine only learns a request is unwanted through abort_request, and the server you wrote is the only part that sees the closed connection.
abort_sequence does mark matches FINISHED_ABORTED, and the scheduler’s next pass then frees their blocks and slots. The gap is that nobody called it.
Preemption puts an evicted request back in line, which costs work, but it happens to live requests short of cache space, not because a client left.
A high limit lets more requests run together, but they would still finish and free their memory. Here the work outlives the test because it was never cancelled.

questions.prompt: Your team serves a few requests per second on eight GPUs. A colleague wants to split prefill and decode, citing DistServe and DeepSeek’s 155 trillion tokens a day. Which test result would best justify the split?
options: Higher peak throughput than the same engine without chunked prefill, at the largest batch
Throughput per GPU close to DeepSeek’s once their cluster figures are scaled to eight GPUs
Lower time to first token on long prompts, with per-token latency left unmeasured
Higher goodput at your latency targets than a single-machine engine with chunked prefill, on your traffic
questions.why: The split pays a handoff cost to remove interference between prefill and decode, and chunked prefill already reduces that interference on one machine. Goodput counts only requests that meet both latency targets, so comparing it on your own traffic against the strongest single-machine option shows whether the trade pays off for you.
questions.hint: DeepSeek’s figures and a peak-throughput run both describe someone else’s conditions. DistServe’s goodput measure, and the chunked-prefill engines that improved after it, suggest what a fair test on your own traffic has to include.
option_feedback: Peak throughput ignores latency targets, and an engine without chunked prefill is the weak baseline the split is easiest to beat.
DeepSeek’s figures come from a design whose smallest efficient unit is 128 GPUs and from a model that compresses its cache heavily, so they don’t scale down to eight GPUs.
Time to first token is half of what goodput checks. A split could improve it while hurting per-token latency, and this test would never show that.
Right. It measures what users feel, on the traffic you actually have, against the colocated design that already attacks the same problem.

transfer: Your first service for a fine-tuned model puts every request in a queue with no size limit, and the engine keeps generating an answer even after the user closes the tab. On a busy afternoon, users at the back of the queue wait over a minute and the GPU stays busy. Explain in your own words what is going wrong and what you would change.
Explains that a queue holds waiting work without adding capacity, so an unlimited one just makes later requests wait longer
Proposes a limit on how much work is admitted or how long a request may wait, and says what happens when it is reached
Explains that abandoned requests must be cancelled so their memory and slot go back to live users

The queue isn’t making the engine any faster; it just lets more requests pile up, so the ones at the back wait longer and longer. I’d cap how many requests we accept and how long one may wait, and send a clear “busy, try again” response when either limit is hit. The second problem is the closed tabs. The engine has no idea the user left, so it keeps generating answers nobody will read, and those requests hold memory and a slot that waiting users need. The server should notice a closed connection or an expired deadline and cancel that request.
LESSONS.takeaway: A service surrounds the engine with admission, cancellation, routing and recovery, and splitting prefill from decode pays only when less interference between them outweighs the cost of moving attention state between machines.

levels.1:
A request spends only part of its life on the GPU.

When a user types a question, a good deal happens before any model calculation starts. A server receives the request, checks that the user is allowed to send it, turns the text into tokens, picks a worker, and may hold the request until a slot frees up. When the model is done, the token IDs are turned back into text and streamed to the user. Each of those steps can add delay, and each can fail.

The program that runs the model calculation is the engine, and a service is the engine plus all of this machinery around it. Keeping the two apart helps when you read a production architecture diagram, and it explains how an open-source engine can be fast and still not be something you could put in front of users. The DeepInfer README, the front page of the public repository, says plainly which parts of DeepSeek’s internal service the release includes and which it leaves out.

Large deployments can give each stage its own workers.

Generating an answer has two phases. During prefill the model reads the whole prompt in one pass, and during decode it extends the answer one token at a time. Because the two load the hardware so differently, a large deployment can run them on separate machines with separate scheduling, an arrangement called disaggregation.

DeepSeek’s Q&A about running DeepInfer in production describes a system that goes one step further and gives multimodal encoding, the work of turning images into something the model can read, a pool of its own. The stages still depend on one another, since decode cannot begin until it holds the numerical state that prefill produced.

Every split creates a handoff.

If one machine processes the prompt and another continues the answer, the attention state has to travel between them. That transfer uses network bandwidth, makes the request depend on a second machine, and adds another place where something can go wrong.

For a large or uneven workload, being able to scale prompt work and answer work independently can repay those costs, while a small workload may do better with both stages on one machine. Which case you are in is something only measurements on your own traffic can tell you.

Queues hold work without adding capacity.

When requests arrive faster than the engine finishes them, the unfinished ones pile up, and if the queue may grow without limit, requests at the back wait longer and longer. So a service needs a policy for how much work to admit, how long a request may wait, and what happens when either limit is reached.

Requests also end early, because a user closes the tab or a timeout fires. The service has to notice and release that request’s memory and scheduler slot, or abandoned work goes on occupying space that live requests need.

A first service can be simple.

For a first service around your fine-tuned model, one compatible engine and a test workload that resembles your real traffic are enough. Once it loads the model you intended and behaves as expected, finding out which step of the request’s journey is slow will teach you more than copying an architecture built for a far larger load.
levels.2:
How DeepInfer’s scheduler admits and evicts requests.

Inside the engine, the decision about which requests run at each step belongs to the scheduler. In DeepInfer it is written in C++ (csrc/engine/scheduler.hpp) and called from Python by LLMEngine.step, the function that runs one engine iteration. Two limits govern admission: max_num_seqs, the number of requests that may run at once, and max_num_batched_tokens, the number of tokens one step may process. The offline example script sets them to 4 and 32,768, and a waiting request is admitted only while both leave room.

Once admitted, every running request needs cache space for its next tokens, which the block manager hands out in fixed-size blocks. When no block is free, the scheduler’s _preempt function evicts a request, which is called preemption. What happens next depends on a setting. With stop_preempted_request on, the evicted request simply ends with status FINISHED_PREEMPTED. Otherwise reset_for_recompute clears its cache bookkeeping and puts it back at the front of the waiting queue, so its prompt and generated tokens are prefilled again later. Requests under a structured-output grammar, which forces the output to match a format such as a JSON schema, are always stopped, because the grammar’s progress cannot be rebuilt that way. The offline LLM wrapper defaults to recomputing.

Cancellation is an explicit call.

Ending a request on purpose goes through LLMEngine.abort_request, which hands the request IDs to the scheduler’s abort_sequence. That function scans both the running and waiting queues and marks the matches FINISHED_ABORTED, and on its next pass the scheduler frees their blocks and slots and returns any image buffers to their shared pool. Nothing calls this for you, though. The engine’s docstring says the release has no online-serving wrapper, meaning no server that accepts user connections, so whatever server you put in front of it has to notice a closed connection or an expired deadline and make the call, or the abandoned request keeps generating.

The hooks for disaggregation exist but are empty.

DeepInfer already names the roles an engine could take in a split deployment. The file deepinfer/engine/engine_type.py lists NORMAL, which runs prompts and completions, PROMPT, which runs only prefill, and COMPLETION, which runs only decode. LLMEngine also has hook methods such as init_pd_split, send_processed_prompts and pe_do_save_kvcache, but their bodies are empty in this release. That fits the README, which lists prefill/decode disaggregation as missing while saying most of the engine functionality it needs is present.

One check in the scheduler’s constructor shows what the split costs. A COMPLETION engine refuses to start unless stop_preempted_request is true, because recomputing an evicted request means prefilling it, and a decode-only engine has no prefill path. Recovery from preemption therefore has to go back through a prefill worker, or the request fails.

What the handoff costs.

For the network between machines, DeepSeek’s production Q&A budgets about 400 Gbps for every 8 GPUs, which is 50 GB/s per machine. Part of what crosses it is small. DeepSeek’s model has some layers with sliding-window attention (SWA), which looks back over only a fixed number of recent tokens, so the stored cache for those layers is a fixed 20 layers × 134 tokens × 528 bytes, about 1.4 MB per sequence, whatever the prompt length. The main block cache grows with the prompt, and the time to move it adds to time to first token unless it overlaps with other work.

The Q&A is careful about which steps of a cache hit can overlap. Matching a prefix is a lookup over a chain of hashes of the token blocks, and because its result decides which machine the request goes to, the request has to wait for it. Fetching the matched blocks from storage into host memory runs asynchronously in another process. Copying them into GPU memory runs layer by layer alongside the forward pass, using RDMA network cards, which write directly into memory so the copy does not occupy the GPU’s compute units. That leaves the prefix lookup as the part of a hit that adds directly to latency.
levels.3:
Disaggregation came from a measured interference problem.

The serving loop that engines use today goes back to Orca, by Gyeong-In Yu and colleagues (OSDI 2022), which scheduled one model iteration at a time so that requests could join and leave a running batch. vLLM, from Woosuk Kwon and colleagues (SOSP 2023), then stored the attention cache in fixed-size pages so those batches could stay large without fragmenting memory (see the PagedAttention paper). DeepInfer descends from it directly, and twenty-one files in its Python package carry a header saying they were derived from vLLM.

Putting prefill and decode in the same batch has a cost, because a long prompt can stall every decoding request that shares its step. DistServe, by Yinmin Zhong and colleagues (OSDI 2024), measured that interference and proposed separate prefill and decode instances. It also changed what gets measured, to goodput: the highest request rate at which a target fraction of requests meet both a time-to-first-token target and a per-token latency target. Splitwise, by Pratyush Patel and colleagues at Microsoft (ISCA 2024), went on to put the two phases on different pools of machines and asked whether each pool should use different hardware.

Engines that keep both phases on one machine improved in the meantime. Sarathi-Serve, by Amey Agrawal and colleagues (OSDI 2024), introduced chunked prefill, which cuts prompts into chunks and mixes them with decode work so that no single step stalls for long, and DeepInfer’s prefill path does a version of this. DeepSeek’s Q&A about running DeepInfer in production describes a cost model, a quadratic curve fitted to measured step times, that picks each chunk’s size to fill a per-step time budget. So the comparison a new deployment should make is between disaggregated serving and a well-tuned single-machine engine with chunked prefill, by goodput on its own traffic, since either system’s peak throughput says little about that choice.

DeepSeek’s production numbers describe one operating point.

The Q&A reports that a single DeepSeek cluster serves 155 trillion tokens a day and earns US$38 per GPU-hour at off-peak prices, and that its load balancers reach about 80% of the throughput of a perfectly balanced offline benchmark. These are DeepSeek’s own figures, not reproduced here, and they come from a design whose smallest efficient unit is 64 prefill GPUs plus 64 decode GPUs, with each decode instance spread across 64 to 128 GPUs using wide expert parallelism. They tell you a lot about running at that scale and little about an eight-GPU deployment.

Several of DeepSeek’s choices also lean on its model. Prefill and decode can sit in different but adjacent data centers because DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, the model DeepInfer serves, compresses its attention cache heavily, so the state sent between buildings is small. The router can ignore prefix affinity, the usual practice of sending a request to the machine that already holds its prefix, because every prefill machine reads from a shared storage cluster and can find any prefix there. A system whose cache lives on the GPU that computed it faces the opposite trade, since routing requests toward their prefix can overload the machine that holds a popular one.

Failure handling is part of the architecture.

The Q&A accepts that restarts take minutes and gets reliability from spare capacity and rerouting instead of faster restarts. A decode engine that receives a shutdown notice gets a one-minute grace period and then forwards its unfinished requests, with their caches, to other decode engines. The platform will not scale in while quota utilization is above 0.8. And because a large expert-parallel instance forms one communication domain, a single failed GPU takes down the whole instance, which on restart is rebuilt at whatever expert-parallel size the healthy GPUs allow. Llumnix, by Biao Sun and colleagues (OSDI 2024), studied migrating running requests between instances as a general scheduling tool, and DeepSeek’s forwarding at shutdown is a narrower use of the same ability.

How long to keep cached prefixes turns out to be an economic choice with measured costs. The Q&A keeps them three days for agent traffic and seven for chatbot traffic, and reports that cutting chatbot traffic to three days would cost 0.5 to 1 percentage point of hit rate, because a small number of chatbot prefixes keep being read over a long period.

Problems this design leaves open.

When models and adapters change under a running fleet, cache keys have to include the model and adapter identity, or a request can read attention state computed by a different model. Balancing load means weighing how many requests a machine holds against their total cache length, and the Q&A says its decode balancer does this by rule of thumb. Published systems also rarely report goodput under bursty arrivals, which is exactly when queue policy has the largest effect on users.

example: You find an output clone inside the generation loop. How do you decide whether it is needed?

The first thing to learn is what the raw output points to. Here, the nearby code and comment concern storage that a later engine step can release or reuse. Appending the object to a list would only keep a reference to that storage, and the contents behind a reference can change.
Next comes timing. If the consumer can read the saved result after the producer has overwritten the buffer behind it, the copy is what keeps the two lifetimes apart.

A test can settle the question before anyone removes the copy. It saves one output, forces the engine to reuse the buffer, and reads the saved output again. Any replacement has to keep that earlier value intact, either by copying or by handing ownership of the buffer to the caller in a way the test can check.

questions.prompt: A new teammate wants to understand how DeepInfer turns a prompt into text, and plans to spend the first week reading the GPU kernels, since those set the speed. What would you suggest instead?
options: Read the configuration flags first, since they decide which kernels run
Run the offline example and follow one request through generate and the engine step
Start with sampler.py, since every generated token passes through it
Read the package in directory order so that every file is seen once
questions.why: Following one request ties each file to something you can watch happen, so the pieces connect as you go. Once you know where the engine step schedules, executes and handles results, the kernels have a place to sit when you open them later.
questions.hint: Kernels, flags and directory order each show you pieces with no question attached. The reading suggests a starting point where every function you meet answers part of something you already want to know.
option_feedback: Flags matter, but without the request path you can’t tell what most of them affect or when.
Right. A traced request shows how the entry point, scheduler and model execution cooperate, and every function you meet answers part of a question you already have.
Sampling is a good detail to study, after you know how a request reaches it. On its own it doesn’t show where its inputs come from.
Directory order covers files without showing how they connect, so the details rarely add up to a picture of what the engine does.

questions.prompt: You add logging inside LLMEngine.step that prints the outputs handled in each call next to the sequences the scheduler just scheduled. They never line up within the same call. Why?
options: The outputs are sorted by request ID, and the scheduler orders sequences differently
The all-reduce mixes in outputs that belong to other data-parallel ranks
Blocks cloned for shared prefixes produce extra outputs for the parent request
With overlap scheduling on, the outputs handled in a step belong to the previous step
questions.why: With zero-overhead scheduling, the default for normal engines, the CPU schedules step N+1 while the GPU is still running step N, so the results processed during a call are the previous step’s. That is also why the loop calls flush_inflight_reqs once at the end to collect the last step still in flight.
questions.hint: Zero-overhead scheduling, the default, lets the CPU plan the next step while the GPU is still running the current one. Consider what that overlap means for the outputs a step hands back.
option_feedback: Sorting by request ID happens once at the end of _run_engine, when results are returned to the caller, not inside each step.
The all-reduce in has_unfinished_requests only combines a yes-or-no answer about remaining work. It doesn’t move outputs between ranks.
Cloned blocks keep a forked request from overwriting shared cache entries. They don’t create outputs of their own.
Right. Scheduling runs one step ahead of execution, so each call handles the results of the step before it.

questions.prompt: A pull request removes the RequestOutput.clone call in _run_engine, citing a profiler trace that shows the copy on every step. The included test compares output shapes and passes. Which test would tell you whether the change is safe?
options: Save one output, run another step, then check that the saved output is unchanged
Run test_batch_invariant.py and confirm that batched and single runs still agree
Benchmark the loop and confirm the step time fell by about the copy’s cost
Compare the dtypes and lengths of the outputs before and after the change
questions.why: step returns objects from a pool that DeferredRelease frees one step later, and the clone is what lets the list in _run_engine outlive that. Only a test that keeps an output across a later step can see whether its contents get overwritten.
questions.hint: Step returns pooled output objects that DeferredRelease frees one step later, and the clone is there because of that. A shape comparison never looks at a saved output after the pool has been reused.
option_feedback: Right. That reproduces the exact lifetime the clone protects, so it separates a safe redesign from one that reads reused memory.
That test checks that batching doesn’t change results. Both of its runs could read the same corrupted pooled objects and still agree.
A faster loop is what the change promises, and it would be just as fast if it returned wrong data.
The reused object keeps its shape and type when its contents are overwritten, so this is the check that already passed.

transfer: A new teammate wants to understand how DeepInfer turns a prompt into text and plans to read every file in the repository in alphabetical order. Suggest a better way to start, and explain how they should keep notes so a colleague can check what they found.
Suggests starting from one concrete request, such as the offline example, and following it through the entry point and the engine step
Explains why a concrete question makes each file easier to understand than reading in file order
Suggests labeling notes as seen in the code, reported by the authors or inferred, and pointing to the fixed commit

Alphabetical order shows you files with no reason to care about them. I’d start with the offline example script, see what it passes in and what it expects back, and then follow that one request: into the LLM class, which admits the request and collects results, and then into the engine’s step, which schedules the work, runs it on the GPU and updates each request. Each function then answers a piece of a question you already have. For notes, I’d mark each line as something seen in the code, something the authors say, or a guess, and link to the exact commit so a colleague can open the same code.
