levels.1:
You can understand one path through a repository before you understand every file.

Opening a large engine repository can feel like walking into the middle of a conversation. There are kernels, the GPU programs that do the arithmetic, along with worker processes, configuration flags and several different objects that each represent a request, and reading the files in alphabetical order rarely shows how they cooperate.

It works better to start from one concrete question, such as what happens when an example script asks the model for a response. If you follow that request from input to output, each function you meet answers a smaller part of the question you already have.

The example script shows the inputs.

A natural starting point is the offline example, examples/offline_inference.py, a short script that loads the model and generates text for a few prompts. It chooses a model, sets how many devices take part, creates the engine and asks for outputs. Most of its options can wait; what you want from it first is what it passes into generation and what it expects back.

The public entry point admits requests and collects results.

The object the example creates is the LLM class in deepinfer/entrypoints/llm.py, whose generation method admits requests and then loops until they finish. Following the call that adds a request, and then the loop that collects its outputs, shows where each request’s identity comes from, which state belongs to it, and how results come back in the right order. These are the engine responsibilities from earlier topics, now visible in code.

One engine step schedules, executes and post-processes.

That loop drives the engine in deepinfer/engine/llm_engine.py. Each call to its step method asks the scheduler which work to run, starts model execution, which proceeds asynchronously on the GPU, and then handles the results by updating each request’s state. Once you have traced that sequence, the kernels are much easier to place when you open them later.

One detail is enough for a first investigation.

A good first detail sits in the entry point itself, where output objects are cloned before the next step can reuse their underlying storage. A copy in a loop that runs every step looks like an easy saving, but the comment beside it ties the copy to storage that a later step reuses, which makes it a clue about how long data lives.

Sampling, in sampler.py, is another good choice, because it keeps ordinary token selection next to the code that verifies draft tokens from speculative decoding. Whichever detail you pick, what you want to pin down is the inputs it receives and the outputs it owns.

It also helps to mark each line of your notes as something you saw in the code, something the authors report, or something you inferred. The source links in this course point to one fixed commit, so a colleague can open exactly the code you read.
levels.2:
From the caller to the engine.

LLM.generate in deepinfer/entrypoints/llm.py accepts either text prompts or prompt_token_ids, along with one SamplingParams object or a list of them, and calls _add_request for each prompt. That function deep-copies the sampling parameters so that one request’s bookkeeping cannot leak into another’s, draws a string request ID from a counter, and, when it is given text, calls tokenizer.encode directly. No chat template is applied anywhere on this path, so laying a conversation out in the format the model was trained on is the caller’s job. The resulting IDs become a one-dimensional np.int32 array.

LLMEngine.add_request wraps those IDs in a Sequence and, for most requests, passes it straight to scheduler.add_sequence. A request with a structured-output schema waits instead while its grammar compiles asynchronously, and a callback enqueues it once the compiled matcher is ready.

The loop and its lockstep condition.

_run_engine keeps going while any request is unfinished, but the way it decides that is worth noticing. has_unfinished_requests answers with an all-reduce, a collective operation in which every rank contributes a value and gets back the combined result, here the maximum across the data-parallel group. So every rank keeps stepping until the last one is done, because the expert-parallel communication inside the model needs every participant, even a rank with nothing left to run.

Each step calls the C++ scheduler, which returns a list of SequenceMetadata and a SchedulerOutputs record saying whether this is a prompt step, which sequences were scheduled or finished, and which cache blocks to clone. Blocks are cloned when a request forks from a shared prefix and must not write into blocks another request is still reading. _execute_model_async_step then asks the workers to run execute_model_step and returns an array of uint64 handles to output objects.

Outputs arrive one step late and expire one step later.

With zero-overhead scheduling on, which is the default for normal engines, the CPU schedules step N+1 while the GPU is still running step N. The docstring of process_output spells out the consequence, which is that the outputs handled during a step belong to the previous one. When no work remains, the loop calls flush_inflight_reqs once to collect the step still in flight, and only then stops.

The output handles point into a RequestOutputPool, and the step docstring says they are released automatically at the next step. The DeferredRelease class does that during the following pre_sampler_sync, overlapped with GPU work. This is why _run_engine calls RequestOutput.clone on every raw output before appending it to a list, since without the clone the list would hold handles to pooled objects that a later step reuses. At the end the results are sorted by integer request ID. With the default decode_sequence=True the caller gets decoded strings, while the examples pass False to keep per-token objects with log-probabilities and draft statistics.

A small kernel worth checking by hand.

The confidence scheduler, schedule_mtp_varlen.py, decides how many of each sequence’s draft tokens the target model verifies in a step. It receives each sequence’s confidence for its draft positions and a total query budget total_q. In its first phase it turns each sequence’s confidences into running products, which estimate the chance that every draft up to that position is accepted, using 0 for a sequence that has no previous step. In the second it ranks every (sequence, position) pair against all the others. Each sequence gets one mandatory slot for the target model’s own token, plus one more for each of its positions that ranks inside the remaining total_q − num_seqs.

A small case makes this concrete. With two sequences of three drafts each and total_q = 5, there are 3 extra slots to hand out. Sequence A has confidences 0.9, 0.8 and 0.5, so its running products are 0.9, 0.72 and 0.36, and sequence B has 0.6, 0.9 and 0.9, giving 0.6, 0.54 and 0.486. The three largest products are A’s 0.9 and 0.72 and B’s 0.6, so A verifies 1 + 2 = 3 positions and B verifies 1 + 1 = 2. Because a running product of numbers no greater than 1 can only fall, and ties go to the lower flat index, the positions a sequence wins always form a prefix of its draft, which is what verification needs, since it stops at the first rejected draft.

Many comments in the repository are in Chinese. Machine translation handles them well, and they often state the invariant the code depends on, as the DeferredRelease docstring does.
levels.3:
The tests show what the authors promise.

Function names tell you what code is responsible for, but the tests under tests/models show which properties DeepSeek thought worth checking on real hardware, and how strictly.

  • test_offline_inference.py compares decode perplexities, a measure of how well the model predicts the text, sample by sample against exact stored baselines in offline_decode_ppl.json, keyed by platform and workload. The examples README describes a separate script that refreshes those baselines once a numerical change has been confirmed as intended.
  • test_batch_invariant.py runs the same prompts batched and one at a time with DEEPINFER_BATCH_INVARIANT=1 and requires identical tokens and log-probabilities.
  • test_kl.py decodes long image-and-text prompts, appends the generated tokens to the prompt, recomputes everything in one prefill, and bounds the KL divergence, a measure of how far one probability distribution is from another, between the two sets of log-probabilities. For the case in the file the bound is 0.
  • test_sampler.py checks that sampled tokens follow the intended distribution, using a randomized probability integral transform and a Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, for greedy sampling and several temperature and top-p settings.

Between them, the tests cover bit-for-bit reproducibility under a flag, agreement between two execution paths, and the statistical correctness of sampling, so a change that touches one path should say which of these it preserves.

A candidate change has to keep the lifetime contract.

The output clone in _run_engine is a good example of judging a change. A profiler shows a copy on every step, and it looks removable, but step returns pooled objects that DeferredRelease frees one step later precisely so the caller has time to read them. Removing the clone safely means replacing that arrangement, for instance by consuming outputs before the next step or by explicitly giving the caller ownership of the pooled object. A test that saves one output, runs another step and reads the saved output again can tell the safe design from the unsafe one, which comparing shapes never could.

The confidence scheduler invites the same reasoning. A useful contribution would be a plain Python reference for it, with running products, a global ranking with ties broken by flat index, and one mandatory slot per sequence, against which the kernel is compared over random confidences, fresh sequences, ties, and budgets at both extremes, from total_q equal to the number of sequences up to every position selected. The kernel is correct when each sequence’s selection is a prefix of its draft and the selections add up to total_q, so those are the two properties the comparison should assert.

DeepInfer’s lineage, and where it departs from vLLM.

The README says DeepInfer was originally built mainly on vLLM, with ideas from SGLang and TensorRT-LLM, and 21 files in the package carry a “Derived from vLLM” header. That makes vLLM’s documentation a help with class names like LLMEngine and SamplingParams, but the resemblance stops in places that matter. DeepInfer’s scheduler has moved to C++, and its asynchronous scheduling follows an overlap design that DeepSeek’s production Q&A credits to SGLang and NanoFlow, two systems that overlap CPU scheduling, computation and communication. The release also supports only one model family on two kinds of accelerator. So what vLLM does is only a guess about what DeepInfer does until the pinned file confirms it.

Some changes are also the wrong size for this repository. The README lists what the release leaves out, namely the cache storage system, disaggregated serving and load balancing, so a pull request adding an online server or a new model architecture raises a design question for the maintainers before anyone reviews the patch. (CONTRIBUTING.md covers formatting and test conventions and says nothing about scope.) A corrected benchmark, a reference test for an existing kernel or a fixed lifetime bug can be judged on its evidence alone.

None of these tests can run without the target hardware. Every one needs SM100 GPUs (NVIDIA’s Blackwell data-center generation) or Huawei Ascend NPUs, plus the full checkpoint. A CPU-runnable reference for small kernels like the confidence scheduler would let far more people check changes, and until one exists, a claim that such a kernel is correct rests on tests few readers can run.

LESSONS.goal: Which files and settings, beyond the weights, you need to run the model you fine-tuned.

The training record should give the intended base revision and the adapter configuration. The tokenizer, the custom prompt format and the stop settings also need to match what training used.

The strongest evidence comes from loading that exact combination in a reference implementation, feeding a deployment path the same tokenized inputs and comparing the results, then checking the behavior you want on a separate evaluation set.

questions.prompt: Your LoRA-tuned chat model loads in a new engine with no errors, and the base revision and adapter are confirmed correct. But its answers run past the end of its turn and sometimes start a fake “User:” line. What is the likeliest cause?

The engine doesn’t support the base model’s architecture
The adapter was merged into the base instead of served beside it
The prompts lack the chat template and stop tokens used in training
questions.why: The weights are right, so the problem sits in what the model is shown and when it is told to stop. A chat model learned to end its turn on particular tokens inside a particular layout, and without that template and those stop rules it keeps writing the conversation forward.
questions.hint: A clean load only shows the weights and adapter fit. The reading lists other things the model learned during training about how its input text is laid out and where a turn ends.
option_feedback: Adapters normally leave out the base weights, and the engine supplies them from the base you load, which you’ve confirmed is the right one.
An unsupported architecture fails when the engine tries to load the model, and this one loaded and runs.
Merging folds the same update into the weights. Its results differ from the unmerged route only in rounding, not in where a turn ends.
Right. The format and stop tokens are part of what the model learned, and changing them shifts behavior while every weight loads cleanly.

questions.prompt: Your adapter was trained with r = 16, lora_alpha = 32 and use_rslora on. A new serving tool loads it without warnings, but on held-out prompts its answers sit between the base model’s and the trained adapter’s. What would you check first?
options: Whether the base revision differs, since renamed modules silently drop part of the update
Whether the tool reads use_rslora, since without it the update runs at a quarter of its trained scale
Whether BF16 rounding in the unmerged route is shrinking the update on every token
questions.why: The rsLoRA flag lives only in adapter_config.json and sets the scale: lora_alpha / √r gives 8 here, while ordinary LoRA’s lora_alpha / r gives 2. The saved matrices are identical either way, so a loader that ignores the flag applies a weaker update and raises no error, which matches a model halfway between base and adapted.
questions.hint: Two adapters with identical saved matrices can be applied at different strengths. The scale comes from settings recorded next to the matrices, and the rank-stabilized variant computes it differently.
option_feedback: Renamed modules fail loudly, because tensor names in the safetensors file encode module paths. A same-named base at another revision loads cleanly but gives different values, not a uniformly weaker effect.
Right. The scale is computed from the configuration, so dropping the flag shrinks the update while every shape still matches.
Rounding differences show up in the last digits and don’t move task results systematically. A consistently weaker adapter points at the scale.

transfer: A teammate plans to hand your fine-tuned model to another team as “the latest base model, plus our adapter folder.” The other team will serve it in a different engine. Explain what could go wrong with that handoff and what you would add to it.
Explains that “latest” can point to a different base that loads cleanly but computes something else
Includes the tokenizer, chat template or input format and stop rules, because the model learned those too
Suggests a short manifest with precision and library versions, plus fixed inputs with expected results to compare against

“Latest” is the biggest risk. If the base is updated, the adapter may still load onto it without any error, because the shapes match, but the numbers underneath are different, so it won’t compute what we trained. I’d write down the exact base revision. I’d also include the tokenizer, the chat format we trained with and the stop tokens, since a model fed text in the wrong layout can ramble or invent extra turns even with perfect weights. Finally I’d add a short manifest with the precision and library versions, and a few fixed test inputs with the scores our reference run produced, so they can check their engine against it.
LESSONS.takeaway: A fine-tuned model is defined by its exact base revision, its adapter or merged weights with their configuration, its tokenizer and input format, its stop rules and its precision settings.

levels.1:
A weights file is only part of the model you trained.

Suppose you fine-tune a base model and want to run the result in an inference engine. It is tempting to think a weights file finishes the job, but the engine also has to know what those numbers mean and how inputs were represented while the model learned them.

It starts with the model’s architecture, the arrangement of layers and calculations that its configuration file describes, which the engine has to support. Fine-tuning changes the learned numbers inside that arrangement and leaves the arrangement itself alone, so an engine that cannot run the base model cannot run your tuned version either.

An adapter may contain only the change.

With LoRA, a common fine-tuning method, what you train is a compact update attached to selected matrices of the base model. The saved adapter usually leaves out the base weights themselves, so running it takes the compatible base as well as the adapter’s configuration and learned values.

“Compatible” is stricter than it sounds. Two revisions of a base model can share every dimension and still hold different learned numbers, so an adapter trained on one may load onto the other without a shape error, and the clean load says nothing about whether it now computes what you trained.

The text format is part of what the model learned.

Before the model sees anything, a tokenizer assigns IDs to pieces of text and to special markers. For a chat-trained model, a chat template first arranges messages and roles into the token sequence the model expects, while a completion model may expect whatever custom format you used during training.

Change any of these and behavior can shift while every weight loads cleanly, which is why the intended tokenizer, input format and stop-token rules belong with the model files.

Enough to rebuild the same computation.

The practical answer is an artifact manifest, a short record of the pieces you used: the exact base revision, the adapter or merged weights, the model configuration, the tokenizer and format, the numerical precision and the relevant library versions. It records a revision that cannot change, because a name like “latest base” points somewhere new every time the base is updated.

You can serve an adapter next to its base or, where the tooling allows, merge its update into a full set of weights. Each route needs its own checks, especially once reduced precision or quantization is involved.

Before any optimization, it pays to load the intended combination in a reference implementation and save a few fixed inputs with their expected scores or task results, so that when an engine later appears to run the model you have something concrete to compare against.
levels.2:
What a LoRA adapter stores.

LoRA leaves each targeted weight matrix W frozen and learns two thin matrices beside it, B with as many rows as W and r columns, and A with r rows and as many columns as W. The adapted weight is W′ = W + s·BA, where r is the rank and s a scaling factor. B starts at zero, so training begins exactly at the base model. Because r is small next to the dimensions of W, the adapter file is a small fraction of the model, and the base matrices it modifies are not in it at all. That is why the adapter is useless without the exact base it was trained against.

The configuration decides what the numbers mean.

Hugging Face’s PEFT library, the usual tool for training LoRA adapters, saves an adapter as a directory that usually holds adapter_config.json and adapter_model.safetensors (see the PEFT LoRA reference). The second file uses the safetensors format, which stores named tensors, and the first records the base model’s name, the rank r, lora_alpha, the target_modules the update attaches to, and variant flags. Those flags change the scale. Ordinary LoRA uses s = lora_alpha / r, while the rank-stabilized variant, switched on by use_rslora, uses s = lora_alpha / √r.

So a loader that ignores a flag fails silently. With r = 16 and lora_alpha = 32, ordinary scaling gives s = 2 and rank-stabilized scaling gives s = 8, so a loader that drops the rsLoRA flag applies a quarter of the trained update while every shape still matches. Errors in the other direction behave differently. The tensor names inside the safetensors file encode module paths, so a base with renamed modules fails loudly, whereas a base with the same names but a different revision loads cleanly with different values underneath.

Merged and unmerged routes compute the same thing differently.

For an input row x, the unmerged route computes xWᵀ + s·(xAᵀ)Bᵀ, paying a little extra work on every token for each adapted matrix. The merged route folds s·BA into W once and then costs nothing extra, but the result is a full checkpoint tied to one adapter. Keeping adapters unmerged lets one copy of the base serve many of them, and vLLM’s adapter serving does this per request. In exact arithmetic the two routes agree, but in BF16 they round at different points, so their outputs can differ in the last digits. A wrong scale or a skipped target module looks different from that rounding noise, because it shifts results systematically and moves task scores.

Serving many adapters on one base also has a consequence for caching. An adapter attached to the key and value projections changes the attention cache for every token, so a prefix cache keyed on token IDs alone could hand one adapter’s cached state to a request running another. Adapter identity has to be part of the cache key.

Text becomes IDs through two separate artifacts.

The tokenizer maps strings to IDs, and the chat template decides which strings the tokenizer sees. For Hugging Face models the template is stored as a Jinja template in tokenizer_config.json, and calling apply_chat_template(messages, add_generation_prompt=True) appends the header that tells a chat model its turn has begun. Leave that out and the model sees a different sequence. The Transformers documentation on chat templates also warns that templated text already contains its special tokens, so tokenizing it again with add_special_tokens=True can duplicate a beginning-of-sequence token.

What DeepInfer does with each artifact.

The LLM constructor in deepinfer/entrypoints/llm.py takes model, tokenizer, revision and tokenizer_revision, so a pinned commit can be passed for both. But _add_request calls tokenizer.encode on raw text and applies no template, and the offline examples use plain few-shot completion prompts. DeepSeek’s chat formatting lives in a separate component, DeepSeek Recipe, which DeepSeek’s production Q&A describes as converting API requests into token sequences. It encodes strings such as <｜User｜> that appear inside user text as ordinary tokens, so pasted text cannot inject control tokens.

The release supports one model family and has no adapter loader. Searching the package for LoRA finds only kv_lora_rank, the compressed attention dimension of DeepSeek’s multi-head latent attention, which is a low-rank projection built into the architecture and has nothing to do with fine-tuning adapters despite the name.

Since each artifact feeds the next, checks go in pipeline order: the configuration and module names first, then token IDs for fixed strings, then logits on fixed IDs, and finally task behavior.

LESSONS.title: What a cache must remember
LESSONS.goal: How the tiny engine’s cache read decides which saved positions attention sees, and how changing where that read starts alters the model’s scores.
LESSONS.recall: You changed how a cache is read and the output still has the right shape. What comparison would convince you the model is still computing the same thing?
LESSONS.predict: A cache read starts one entry too late. Before running anything, guess whether the generated tokens go wrong right away, a few steps later, or possibly not at all on a short prompt.
example: We process input IDs [1, 4]. These numbers name tokens, and the keys and values saved in the cache are computed from them.
The first input creates the entry at position 0. With only one entry, attention gives it all of the weight, and the cached path and the full-prefix reference use the same information.

The second input adds an entry at position 1. Starting the read at 0 keeps both entries. Attention splits its weight between the two saved values, and the cached scores still agree with the reference.

Now only the read boundary changes, to 1. Position 0 is still stored, but attention no longer receives it, so the remaining entry gets all of the weight. One next-token score shows what the missing contribution does to the numbers.

questions.prompt: A teammate’s cache read uses cache.keys[1:] and cache.values[1:] once the cache holds more than one entry. The code runs and the slices always have equal lengths. Compared with a full recomputation, at which input do the next-token scores first differ?
options: The first input, since the read skips an entry from the start
The second input, when the cache first holds two entries
The third input, once enough history is missing to change the scores
None, since the keys and values are still read as matching pairs
questions.why: With one entry the condition is false and attention sees everything. When the second input arrives, the read starts at position 1 and position 0’s value drops out of the mixture, so the scores change at once.
questions.hint: A slice starting at 1 leaves out position 0. That omission can only matter once the cache holds position 0 together with at least one other entry.
option_feedback: With a single saved entry the read takes the whole cache, so the first input is computed exactly as the reference does.
Right. That is the first moment there is an entry to skip, and leaving out position 0 changes the attention mixture immediately.
One missing entry already changes the weighted mix of values, so there’s no threshold to wait for.
Paired slices only show that each key still has its value. They don’t show that the history attention needs is all there.

questions.prompt: With broken_offset on, a test generates greedy tokens for the prompt 1, 4, 2, 8 and they match the reference’s choices. A colleague concludes the cache is fine. What does the test actually show?
options: That the bug is harmless here, since a missing entry would change the chosen tokens
That the bug has faded, since the score difference shrinks by the fourth token
Little, since the top token can survive a shifted score; comparing all 16 scores catches it
questions.why: Picking the highest-scoring token throws away most of what the model computed. The broken read shifts scores by about 0.165 at the second position, which may leave the winner unchanged, while a comparison of all 16 scores at every position catches the error the first time it occurs.
questions.hint: Greedy decoding keeps only the highest-scoring token at each step. A shifted score elsewhere in the list of 16 can leave that choice unchanged.
option_feedback: A changed score only changes the chosen token if it reorders the top of the list, so matching tokens can hide a real error.
The difference shrinks because each new entry dilutes the missing one’s share of attention, but position 0 is still missing from every later step.
Right. Matching tokens are weak evidence, and comparing every score at every position finds the error at the first prefix where it exists.

questions.prompt: You plant a bug in the tiny engine that divides attention scores by 12 instead of √12 inside the shared attention function. All 218 reference checks still pass. Why, and what would catch it?
options: The 10⁻¹⁰ tolerance is too loose; a tighter one would catch it
Random weights hide scaling errors; a trained checkpoint would catch it
The interleaved-request check skips attention; extending it would catch it
Both paths call the same attention code; a hand-computed two-position case would catch it
questions.why: full_logits and cached_step share input_vector, attention and finish_block, so a mistake inside shared code shows up identically in both and every comparison agrees. Catching it takes a check that doesn’t route through that code, such as arithmetic worked out by hand on a tiny case or an invariant the output must satisfy.
questions.hint: The cache-offset bug was caught because the cached path and the full-prefix path disagreed. Ask which code those two paths have in common.
option_feedback: The two paths would agree exactly, so no tolerance, however tight, would see a difference.
Both paths would still run the same wrong scaling on a trained model, so their scores would still match each other.
That check compares each request with its own reference, and both still go through the same shared attention code.
Right. Differential testing can’t see a bug that both implementations share, so an independent check is needed.

transfer: Your teammate changes the tiny engine so the cache read starts at 1 instead of 0, and says: “The keys and values still have the same length, so nothing is lost.” Explain in your own words what is actually left out, when the next-token scores would first change, and why equal lengths don’t prove the change is safe.
Identifies that position 0’s key and value are dropped from what attention reads
Explains that the scores first differ at the second input, when the cache first holds two entries
Explains that equal lengths only show keys and values are still paired, not that all of the needed history is there

Starting the read at 1 skips position 0, so the first token’s key and value never reach attention. Nothing changes while the cache has just one entry, but at the second input attention should mix both saved values and now sees only one, so the next-token scores change from there on. The equal lengths are a red herring: both slices lose the same entry, so they still line up as pairs, but the history attention needed is missing. The right check is to compare the scores with a full recomputation, not to look at array sizes.
LESSONS.takeaway: Starting the cache read at index 1 drops position 0 from attention while key and value lengths stay equal, so only comparing scores against the full-prefix reference reveals the bug.

activity.title: Repair the highlighted cache read.
activity.intro: The cache now has positions 0 and 1. Change the highlighted start value, predict which entries attention will receive, and run the selected branch of the actual CPU engine.

levels.1:
The code above reads the cache in a tiny engine. A cache lets the engine skip recomputing earlier tokens, but attention still has to read every piece of history it needs, and a one-line change to this read can drop part of that history without changing the length of any array.

What a slice selects.

Python counts positions from zero, and the colon in a slice means “from here to the end,” so with two saved entries [0:] selects positions 0 and 1 while [1:] selects only position 1. The stored arrays keep their full size either way. The slice only decides which entries the calculation receives.

What each entry stores.

Each saved entry holds a key and a value, two vectors of numbers computed from a token and its position. The current token supplies the query, named q in the code, and attention compares it with each visible key, then uses the resulting weights to mix the matching values.

Leave an entry out of the read and its contribution to that mixture disappears. The rest of the model then works from a different mixture and produces different next-token scores, even though the key and value slices still have equal lengths.

Where the scores first change.

Nothing goes wrong while the cache holds a single entry, so the difference first appears when the second input arrives. “See an example” shows the actual entries and attention weights at each position, and “Try it” lets you change the highlighted value, predict which entries remain, run your version, and then explain why your repair is justified.

The model behind the lab uses random weights and numbered tokens, so its output will never read as fluent language. Its purpose is to make each step of the calculation visible.
levels.2:
The tiny engine’s shapes.

The lab’s model, tiny_engine.py, is a single transformer block with random weights: width 12, a vocabulary of 16 token IDs, one attention head, learned position vectors, a residual connection and a small tanh MLP. input_vector adds a token’s 12-number embedding to its position’s 12-number vector, and three 12 × 12 matrices turn that input into a query, a key and a value. After n tokens, then, the cache holds n keys and n values of 12 numbers each.

From there attention_weights scores each visible key against the query as a dot product divided by √12 and applies softmax, which gives one weight per visible position with the weights summing to 1. attention returns the weighted sum of the visible values, again 12 numbers, and finish_block applies the output projection, the residual, a 24-wide hidden layer and the projection back. Finally output_logits multiplies by a 16 × 12 output matrix to produce 16 next-token scores.

Two paths to the same scores.

The reference, full_logits, recomputes the query, key and value at every position of a prefix and lets position i attend to positions 0 through i. Producing scores for each new token this way repeats all the earlier work, which is exactly what a cache exists to avoid. cached_step computes the query, key and value for the new token only, appends the key and value to the cache, and attends over the stored lists.

Because both paths perform the same scalar operations on the same numbers in the same order, the lab can demand agreement to within 10⁻¹⁰. A vectorized port would sum in a different order, and its tolerance would then have to allow for double-precision rounding over that many additions.

Where the broken read first shows up.

With broken_offset on, the read starts at 1 once the cache holds more than one entry. On the lesson’s prompt, token IDs 1, 4, 2, 8, the scores match exactly at prefix length 1, because the cache has one entry and the condition is false. At length 2 the reference splits attention between positions 0 and 1, while the broken read sees only position 1 and gives it weight 1.0, and the largest score difference is about 0.165. Position 0 stays missing at lengths 3 and 4, where the differences are about 0.097 and 0.059. They shrink because each new entry dilutes the missing one’s share of attention, but every later step is still computed without position 0.

Watching the generated text would be a weaker check. The highest-scoring token can survive a 0.165 shift in some scores, so a broken cache can keep producing the right next token for a while, whereas comparing all 16 scores at every position catches the error at the first prefix where it exists.

What the reference checks cover.

The “Try it” panel runs reference_checks, which reports 218 comparisons. Most of them, 177, compare cached and full-prefix scores after every position for three random seeds and prompt lengths 1, 2, 7, 16 and 33. Another 15 compare six-token greedy continuations. Two interleaved requests with separate caches are each compared to their own reference, 24 comparisons that would catch a cache shared by mistake. One hand-built rank-2 update to the output matrix is applied both separately and merged into the weights, the only adapter-like case, since the tiny engine loads no trained adapters. The last check confirms that a model with a maximum context of 2 rejects a third token without appending it to the cache.

A scheduler extension would be tested the same way, by comparing each request against its own independent generation, including requests that finish early and a new request that takes over a freed slot.
levels.3:
The same oracle runs in DeepInfer’s test suite.

The comparison you ran in the lab, cached decoding against a full recomputation, is also how DeepInfer’s tests/models/test_kl.py checks the production engine, using it as an oracle at far larger scale. The test builds image-and-text prompts of 16,384 tokens and decodes 1,024 tokens per prompt, forcing the tokens to a fixed golden sequence so the run does not depend on sampling. It then appends the generated tokens to the prompt, runs the whole sequence again as one prefill, and asks for the log-probability of every token. The test then checks that the prompt log-probabilities are identical across the two runs, and the KL divergence between decode-time and prefill-time log-probabilities must not exceed max_kl, which is 0 for the case in the file. The run uses speculative drafting, context parallelism and expert parallelism over 8 GPUs, with DEEPINFER_BATCH_INVARIANT=1 set.

That flag is what makes a bound of zero possible. Without batch invariance, a sum can be split differently depending on how many tokens share the batch, so a decode step and a long prefill add the same numbers in different orders and round differently. Horace He and colleagues at Thinking Machines Lab described this source of nondeterminism in 2025 and showed kernels that remove it. DeepInfer’s README offers batch-invariant inference on NVIDIA hardware only, and anywhere else some nonzero tolerance is unavoidable. For those cases deepinfer.testing.cal_diff reports cosine difference, root-mean-square error, the largest single difference and KL divergence, which together describe both the size and the shape of a disagreement.

Two implementations can share a bug.

Checking one implementation against another is called differential testing, a name William McKeeman gave the practice in 1998, and the tiny engine shows where it is weak. full_logits and cached_step call the same input_vector, attention and finish_block, so a wrong scaling factor inside attention would appear in both paths and pass every comparison. The cache-offset bug is caught only because it lives in the one line the two paths do not share.

Covering that gap takes checks that do not route through shared code. A hand-computed case with two positions and tiny integer weights tests the arithmetic directly. Invariants catch whole classes of error, for instance that attention weights sum to 1 and that the scores for a prefix do not depend on tokens after it. A metamorphic test changes something that should not matter, such as which other request shares the batch, and requires the output to stay the same, which is what the lab’s interleaved-request check does.

Keeping the oracle as the engine grows.

Each natural extension of the tiny engine changes one mechanism and comes with its own test. A NumPy or PyTorch port of the arithmetic keeps the scalar version as the oracle, with a tolerance chosen for the new summation order. Continuous admission with two active slots keeps the caches separate and compares every request with its independent generation, including early finishes and slot reuse. Paged storage needs tests at lengths of one page minus one, exactly one page and one page plus one, along with page reuse, and an explicit maximum-context policy, reject or truncate, needs a test of its own, since silently changing what attention sees changes behavior.

DeepInfer’s KL test needs eight GPUs and the full checkpoint, while the tiny engine runs in milliseconds on a laptop and can be rerun after every change.

LESSONS.title: Serve your fine-tuned model
LESSONS.goal: How to move a fine-tuned model into a compatible engine and check, one change at a time, that it still computes what you trained.
LESSONS.recall: Your fine-tuned model answers well in a notebook. What would you record now so that, after moving it into an engine, you could tell whether the engine changed anything?
LESSONS.predict: You start a server with your adapter, send a request that names it, and get HTTP 200 with the adapter’s name echoed back. Before reading on, guess whether that shows the adapter’s update was applied.
example: The endpoint returns HTTP 200 and reports your adapter’s name. What further evidence would show that it runs your adapted model?
The first check is which base and adapter files the engine actually loaded. A label in the response can name the intended configuration without proving which learned values are in memory.

Next, fixed inputs are compared against the adapted reference. They should include a held-out task where the adapted model behaves noticeably differently from the base, plus numerical predictions where the engine exposes them.

Once that behavior is established, concurrent requests, limits and restart or reload behavior can be tested. These service checks answer different questions from the model comparison and cannot replace it.

questions.prompt: You move your fine-tuned model into a new engine and, in the same change, switch to 4-bit quantization and rewrite the prompt formatting for the engine’s API. Task scores drop by 6 points. What can you conclude?
options: Quantization caused it, since that change is the one most likely to cost quality
The engine caused it, since the weights and adapter themselves did not change
Not much yet, until each change is rerun on its own against the reference
The new formatting caused it, since the model never saw that layout in training
questions.why: Three things changed at once, and any one of them, or a combination, could explain the drop. Making one change at a time against the saved reference turns a single unexplained number into a result you can trace to a cause.
questions.hint: Three things changed together: the engine, the numerical format and the prompt formatting. Count how many of them could, on their own, explain a lower score.
option_feedback: Quantization is a likely suspect, but the formatting rewrite could cost as much on its own, and this run can’t separate them.
Unchanged weights don’t mean unchanged inputs or numbers. The formatting and precision both changed in the same run.
Right. With three changes in one step, the drop can’t be pinned on any of them, so the comparison has to be redone one change at a time.
A format mismatch can hurt a model badly, which makes it a reasonable guess, but quantization and the engine changed in the same run.

questions.prompt: You serve your adapter in vLLM with --enable-lora. Requests name the adapter in the model field, and responses echo the name back. Which result shows the adapter’s update is actually being applied?
options: On prompts where the base and adapted references differ, the engine matches the adapted one
The server log lists the adapter path among the LoRA modules it loaded at startup
The response’s model field returns the adapter’s name in place of the base model’s
On generic prompts, teacher-forced log-probabilities closely match the adapted reference
questions.why: A name in the log or the response shows that the server accepted the adapter, not that its numbers changed the computation. Only prompts on which the two references clearly disagree can tell an applied adapter from a silent fall-back to the base.
questions.hint: A name in the response or a path in the log shows the request was accepted, not that the adapter’s numbers were used. Look for the result that would come out differently if the engine were quietly running the base model.
option_feedback: Right. If the engine matched the base row on those prompts instead, you’d know the update never took effect.
Loading an adapter at startup doesn’t show that requests are routed through it, or that it was applied at the right scale.
The echoed name shows only that the server accepted the name, not that the adapter’s values went into the computation.
On generic prompts the base and adapted models may agree almost exactly, so a close match there can’t tell the two apart.

transfer: Your teammate moved the fine-tuned model to a new engine, switched it to a smaller numerical format, and changed how prompts are formatted, all in one go. The endpoint returns HTTP 200 and the answers look reasonable. Your manager asks whether it is still the model you trained. Explain what you would tell them and what you would do next.
Explains that an HTTP 200 and reasonable-looking answers don’t show the adapter is active or the model behaves as in the reference
Proposes separating the changes and checking them one at a time against a reference run
Mentions fixing the inputs as token IDs, with the same settings, so the reference and the engine see the same thing

I’d say we don’t know yet. A 200 only means the endpoint answered, and reasonable answers could come from the base model with our adapter silently missing. Because three things changed at once, any difference we find can’t be pinned on one of them. I’d first run the model in a reference implementation and save its results on fixed test prompts, stored as token IDs with the same settings. Then I’d move to the new engine with the original format and compare, and only after that matches try the smaller numerical format as its own experiment.
LESSONS.takeaway: A first deployment compares the adapted model in a reference implementation with the same model in the engine on fixed token IDs, before adding a server, concurrent requests or quantization.

Give both paths the same token IDs and generation rules. Identical visible text can become different inputs under different formatting.

levels.1:
You want two things from a first deployment: that it runs the model you actually trained, and that it runs it efficiently. The first has to be settled before speed can justify any change, because if you change both at once and the output differs, you cannot tell whether the model files, the input format, the numerical format or the engine caused it.

The engine has to support the model’s calculations.

So the starting point is the exact architecture and configuration of your base model, which the engine has to support along with the adapter path you use and the numerical format you plan to serve. vLLM’s list of supported models is one place to look this up, since vLLM is a widely used open-source engine that covers many architectures.

DeepInfer, the advanced case study in this course, is built around DeepSeek’s own models and makes no promise to run every model fine-tuned from every base. A compatible general-purpose engine is usually the more practical first home for your model.

Fixed inputs.

Using the correct tokenizer and the training-time format, you turn your test prompts into prompt IDs and record them with the stop rules and generation settings. All of that stays fixed whenever the reference and the engine are compared.

Fixing the IDs, and not just the visible text, avoids a common confusion, because two systems can show the same question on screen and still run different token sequences if each formatted it differently.

The model is checked before an API goes around it.

The first run loads the intended base plus adapter, or the intended merged checkpoint, in a direct reference implementation. It saves numerical predictions where possible and scores examples from a held-out set, cases kept out of training that show how the model behaves beyond the examples it was fitted to.

The compatible engine then runs on the same inputs. The strongest comparison is next-token probabilities, where the engine exposes them, followed by greedy outputs under controlled settings and then the task results you care about. When only the weaker comparisons are available, your notes should say so.

Complexity comes one change at a time.

Once offline generation matches, a local endpoint comes next, then concurrent requests, and after that tests of limits, cancellation, a range of input lengths and reloading. Quantization is an experiment of its own, so that any change in quality has one identifiable cause.

An HTTP 200 response tells you the endpoint answered. It cannot show that your adapter was active or that the model still behaves as it did in the reference, which is why the artifact identities and reference comparisons are kept next to the service measurements.
levels.2:
The comparison table comes before the server.

It helps to lay the first deployment out as a table with four rows: the base model in a reference implementation, the adapted model in that reference, the adapted model in the engine, and optionally a quantized engine run. Each neighboring pair differs in one thing. The gap between the first two rows is what fine-tuning changed, the gap between the second and third comes from execution, and the gap between the third and fourth comes from numerical representation.

Teacher-forced log-probabilities are the strongest comparison.

Comparing generated text has a weakness, since one early disagreement sends the two systems down different paths and every later token differs too. Teacher forcing avoids that by giving each system a fixed prompt plus a fixed continuation, for example the reference model’s greedy output, as one input, and asking for the log-probability it assigns to every token. Every position then sees identical inputs. In vLLM the prompt_logprobs field of SamplingParams returns these values for the prompt tokens, and DeepInfer’s own tests use the same pattern, with test_kl.py passing golden_token_ids to force a continuation and prompt_logprobs=True to read back the recomputed values. The useful summary is the largest and mean absolute difference per token, plus the positions where the top-ranked token changes.

When an engine exposes no log-probabilities, greedy continuations under fixed settings are the next best thing, and the first position where they diverge is what to record. A divergence at a near-tie between two tokens is weak evidence of a bug, while one at a position where the model was confident is strong evidence. Task scores on held-out data come last, because they answer a different question, whether the model still does its job, which neither of the other comparisons can.

Checking that the adapter is active.

vLLM serves adapters when started with --enable-lora and a --lora-modules entry mapping a name to an adapter path (see vLLM’s LoRA serving guide). A request selects the adapter by putting that name in its model field, and the response echoes the name back, which shows the name was accepted but not that the adapter’s numbers were applied. Held-out prompts on which the base and adapted references clearly differ settle the question. If the engine matches the base row on them, the update never took effect.

Where DeepInfer fits.

The release supports DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on NVIDIA SM100 GPUs and Huawei Ascend 950 NPUs, and it documents no adapter path. Even its low-precision formats were chosen together with that model. DeepSeek’s production Q&A lists 4-bit floating-point (FP4) variants for the main cache, for the smaller cache the model uses to choose which earlier tokens to attend to, and for the routed expert weights. For most fine-tuned models, then, DeepInfer is reading material, and the first deployment runs on a general engine with documented support for the architecture.

Service checks come after the table matches.

Only then is the endpoint tested under mixed prompt lengths, concurrent requests, cancellation mid-stream, requests at the context limit, and a restart or reload. After a reload the fixed inputs are run again and compared with the saved rows, since a reload is another chance to load the wrong files.

LESSONS.title: Test a performance claim
LESSONS.goal: How to tell whether an engine change helped your workload, and how to record the evidence so that someone else can rerun it.
LESSONS.recall: A chart shows another engine at twice your tokens per second. What would you want to know about how that number was produced before believing it applies to you?
LESSONS.predict: DeepSeek estimates that verifying fewer draft tokens raises throughput at its production load. Before reading on, guess whether the same change could make a lightly loaded deployment slower.
example: DeepInfer’s README reports decode throughput from its benchmark script. Before comparing that figure with your own deployment, what does it actually count?

The script computes decode throughput as steps per second × requests × (1 + draft length). Each request is credited with the target’s own token plus every draft token at every step, 6 tokens at the default draft length of 5, whatever fraction of drafts the target accepted. The README calls this full-acceptance accounting, so the figure is an upper bound.

Real acceptance is lower. DeepSeek’s production Q&A reports accepted lengths of about 3.1 to 3.3 tokens for 5-token drafts, and acceptance on your fine-tuned model and traffic could differ again. The plotting script can rescale results by an assumed acceptance rate, and it refuses to do so for runs whose step counts already reflect acceptance.

The benchmark also measures steady state with every request present from the start, after warmup and with profiling off. It says nothing about queueing under real arrivals. Comparing it with your deployment means measuring accepted tokens, latency percentiles and arrivals on your own workload under the same accounting.

questions.prompt: A blog post shows an engine at twice your tokens per second. Their test sent many short prompts that share one long system prompt. Your users send long documents that share nothing. What is the most reasonable reading?
options: Expect about 2×, since the model and hardware are the same
Expect a loss, since engines tuned for short prompts are slower on long ones
Treat it as untested for you, since cache hits and lengths may explain the gain
Expect more than 2×, since long prompts give the engine more work to batch
questions.why: Their workload hit a shared prefix on almost every request and used short prompts, and both can raise throughput on their own. Your traffic changes both conditions, so the chart says little about your case until you run the comparison on a workload like yours.
questions.hint: Their speedup came from a particular workload: short prompts that share a cached prefix. Your users send long documents with nothing shared, so the cache and the request lengths both differ.
option_feedback: The same model and hardware can behave very differently when request lengths and cache state change.
The chart shows nothing about long prompts either way, so predicting a loss goes as far beyond the evidence as predicting the gain.
Right. The gain belongs to the measured workload until you reproduce it under yours.
Longer prompts change where the time goes, but nothing in the result says the gain grows. It was measured under different conditions.

questions.prompt: Two engineers report p99 inter-token latency for the same benchmark run, 140 ms and 65 ms. Both did the arithmetic correctly. What most likely explains the gap?
options: One took the p99 of all token gaps pooled; the other, of each request’s mean gap
One measured latency per GPU and the other per server
One counted input tokens and the other counted output tokens
questions.why: The p99 of pooled gaps is set by the worst 1% of individual gaps, which may all come from a few long requests, while the p99 of per-request means describes the slowest 1% of users. Both are legitimate numbers, so a latency target has to say which one it means.
questions.hint: Inter-token latency can be summarized over every token gap pooled together or over each request’s average gap. The reading shows these two populations can give very different p99s from the same run.
option_feedback: Right. Same run, different populations: one describes the worst moments, the other the worst-served users.
Per-GPU and per-server scope changes throughput figures. A gap between two tokens of one request is the same however many devices you divide by.
Input and output tokens change a throughput count. Inter-token latency is measured between output tokens, so this choice doesn’t apply.

questions.prompt: You enable confidence-scheduled verification after reading DeepSeek’s estimate of a 4 to 7% throughput gain. Your deployment decodes about 16 sequences per GPU, and throughput drops slightly. What best explains it?
options: Your drafter is less accurate, so the scheduler ends up verifying too many drafts
At low load, verifying a draft costs almost nothing, so skipping drafts mainly loses accepted tokens
The profiler was left on, and it inflates step times by nearly 50% at small batch sizes
Confidence scheduling needs 64-way expert parallelism and degrades on smaller setups
questions.why: DeepSeek’s own estimates run from −1.5% at 16 sequences per GPU to +11% at 96, with the 4 to 7% figure belonging to its production load of about 60. With few sequences the GPU has spare compute, so cutting verification saves little and occasionally gives up a token that would have been accepted.
questions.hint: DeepSeek’s Q&A estimates the gain at several loads, from 16 sequences per rank up to 96, and its headline figure is for about 60. Check where your deployment sits on that curve and what extra drafts cost there.
option_feedback: A weaker drafter would lower its confidences and lead the scheduler to verify fewer drafts, not more, and the drop here matches what DeepSeek itself estimates at this load.
Right. The saving only turns into throughput when verification competes with other requests for compute, which happens at higher loads.
A profiler left on would distort timing, but the result you saw is what DeepSeek’s own figures predict at 16 sequences per GPU.
The 64-way setup is where DeepSeek’s estimates were made. What changes the sign of the result is the number of sequences per GPU.

transfer: A colleague reports that a configuration change doubled tokens per second for your fine-tuned model. They tested many short prompts that shared a long cached prefix, on a different GPU from production. Your users send long documents and care about how long they wait for the first word. Explain why you can’t yet expect the same gain and what the result would need to include.
Explains that the workload, such as prompt length and cached prefixes, can produce the gain on its own
Points out that throughput alone misses what users feel, such as the wait for the first token and the slow tail
Asks for a reproducible record: hardware, model and code versions, settings and the measurement commands

Their test was close to the best case: short prompts sharing a prefix the engine had already cached, so a lot of the work was skipped. Our users send long documents with nothing shared, so the same change may help less or not at all. Also, tokens per second doesn’t tell us how long someone waits for the first word, or how slow the worst requests get. Before trusting it, I’d want them to record the exact model, code revision, GPU, settings and commands, and rerun it on a workload like ours, reporting first-token wait and tail latency along with throughput.
LESSONS.takeaway: A speed claim can be judged only with its baseline, workload, latency metric, correctness promise and measurement method, and DeepSeek’s own estimate for confidence-scheduled verification changes sign with the number of sequences per GPU.

activity.title: Make one change and decide what the evidence supports.
activity.intro: Use your own model experiment if you have one. Until then, write a proposed experiment and label every unmeasured result “not measured.” Choose one mechanism from the course; you can start applying it without a separate final project.

fields.label: What workload and user requirement will you keep fixed?
fields.placeholder: Prompt/output lengths, request arrivals, concurrency, cache state, hardware, numerical format, quality requirement, and a latency target.

fields.label: What one change will you try, and why?
fields.placeholder: The trace or other evidence suggests… I will change… I expect this tradeoff…

fields.label: What did the matched comparison actually show?
fields.placeholder: Correctness checks and tolerance, before/after timing and useful throughput, memory, task quality, and limits. Write “not measured” for missing evidence.

fields.label: Would you keep the change, and where might it fail?

compare: State exactly which model files, engine revision, hardware, inputs, numeric format, and cache conditions ran.
Use observed evidence to name a limiting resource. A plausible explanation alone is a hypothesis.
Change one mechanism, repeat the correctness checks, and rerun the same workload. Explain any remaining differences between configurations.
Keep latency and task quality requirements visible. A larger combined output rate does not establish lower user waiting time or equal cost.
A plan is useful before you have hardware, but it is still a plan. A decision about a measured gain needs the actual results and their limits.
activity.example: If a trace suggests repeated weight reads dominate my workload, I might test a different batch policy while keeping the model, hardware, inputs, numerical format, and cache state fixed. I would rerun reference checks and compare user waiting times, useful output rate, memory, and task quality under the same arrival pattern. I would keep the change only if the relevant requirement improves without an unacceptable regression. Before collecting those measurements, I would record this as a proposed experiment.

levels.1:
A benchmark result depends on what it compared.

Imagine a benchmark that reports twice as many tokens per second, and you would like the same gain for your fine-tuned model. Before chasing it, you need to know what was compared and which conditions produced the result.

The GPU count, numerical format, request lengths, batch size and cache state can each move that number, and when several of them changed together, the chart cannot tell you which one produced the gain.

Every result needs a description of the workload.

What kind of work the engine actually did depends on the workload: how long prompts and outputs are, how requests arrive, how many run at once and whether their prefixes are already cached. A configuration that does well on many short requests can struggle with a few long-context ones, even though both workloads run the same model.

Latency and quality requirements belong in the comparison.

If users need an answer that streams smoothly, total throughput is not enough. What matters then is the wait before the first token, the gaps between later tokens and the slow tail of requests, along with which percentile has to meet your target.

The correctness promise belongs in the comparison too. An approximation that lowers task quality is a different trade from an exact rewrite that removes redundant work, and a headline speedup should say which kind it is.

What a reproducible result records.

For someone else to tell what ran and what the numbers include, a result has to carry the exact model and adapter identities, code revision, hardware, library versions, precision settings, workload, warmup procedure and measurement commands.

A disappointing result can tempt you to try a different workload. That is a new experiment and should be labeled as one, and a finding that an optimization helps one case and hurts another is worth recording in its own right.

The final project for your own model.

The notes and checks from earlier topics lead to one justified code or configuration change for a supported deployment of your fine-tuned model. The write-up shows the reference comparison, the evidence for the bottleneck, the change itself and the repeated benchmark, and it says both how large the gain is and where it stops.
levels.2:
Each latency number needs its population.

Two latencies describe what a user of a streaming service feels. Time to first token (TTFT) runs from a request’s arrival to its first output token, so it includes queueing and prefill, and inter-token latency (ITL) is the gap between successive tokens of one request. A percentile of either only means something once you say what it is a percentile of. The p99 of 10,000 pooled token gaps is set by the worst 100 gaps, which may all come from a few long requests, while the p99 of per-request mean gaps describes the slowest 1% of users, so a target has to say which one it means.

Throughput has the same problem with units and scope. Tokens per second per GPU or per server, input or output tokens, and all requests or only those that met their latency targets each give a different number from the same run.

How DeepInfer’s benchmark measures.

DeepInfer’s benchmark script, examples/benchmark.py, which the examples README documents, measures prefill and decode separately, each at steady state. For prefill it skips 5 warmup chunks and divides the tokens of 10 steady intervals by their duration and the number of devices, giving tokens per second per GPU. For decode it reports avg_SPS, steps per second over 60 clean intervals after 50 warmup steps and 60 logged steps, dropping intervals that collide with the periodic flush of expert-load statistics.

Decode throughput is then computed as avg_SPS × decode_num_requests × (1 + nextn) / cp, where nextn is the number of draft tokens per step and cp is the context-parallel size. The README calls this full-acceptance accounting, because each request is credited with 1 + nextn tokens per step, 6 at the default draft length of 5, however many drafts the target model actually accepted, so the figure is an upper bound. The plotting script sweep/plot_pareto.py can rescale it by τ = 1 + nextn × a for an assumed fraction a of drafts accepted. At a = 0.75 that gives τ = 4.75, so the full-acceptance figure is about 1.26 times the rescaled one. The script refuses to rescale runs with confidence-scheduled verification on, because their step counts already reflect acceptance.

The README also warns about the profiler. With profiling on, step times inside the trace can be inflated by nearly 50% at batch size 1, so traces are for seeing which kernels run and never for computing speed. Even after the profiler exits a slowdown of about 7 to 11% remains, which is why the profiler runs at the very end. For a similar reason, the prefill plot uses measured step times, since dividing batch size by throughput would assume every step was full.

A matched comparison.

Testing your own change means holding everything else fixed: the model and adapter revisions, code revision, hardware and topology, library versions, numeric formats, the distributions of prompt and output lengths, the arrival process, warmup, cache state and sample count. The comparison records failures, p50, p95 and p99 TTFT and ITL, useful throughput, peak memory, and task score with its tolerance. Perfect matching is not always possible, and when it isn’t, the write-up lists the remaining differences and narrows its conclusion to what the data supports.

Configurations are then compared at a matched requirement. Only those that meet the latency and quality targets stay in, and the survivors are ranked by throughput or cost. Cost needs real prices and comparable useful work, which a GPU count does not provide.

The order of work keeps causes separable. Correctness comes first, then a trace that shows the limiting resource, then one change, a second correctness check, and a rerun of the same workload.
levels.3:
DeepSeek’s estimated gain changes sign with load.

In speculative decoding a fast drafter proposes several tokens and the target model checks, or verifies, all of them in one step. DeepInfer normally verifies 5 drafts per sequence, and its confidence scheduler, described in the code topic, verifies fewer for sequences whose drafts look unlikely to be accepted. DeepSeek’s Q&A about running DeepInfer in production estimates the effect from benchmark data on a deployment with 64-way expert parallelism and 64-way data parallelism. The average number of drafts verified per step falls from 5.00 to between 3.2 and 4.4, while the average number of tokens accepted barely moves, from 3.29 to 3.20.

Whether that saving turns into throughput depends on how many sequences each rank, one GPU’s share of the deployment, is decoding at once. The estimated change is −1.5% at 16 sequences per rank, +1.6% at 32, +5.4% at 60 and +11.0% at 96, and DeepSeek’s headline figure of +4 to 7% is for its production load of about 60. The reason is that with few sequences the GPU has spare compute, so verifying an extra draft costs almost nothing and skipping drafts mainly loses the occasional accepted token. With many sequences, verification competes with other requests for compute, and dropping unlikely drafts frees capacity. A gain reported for this mechanism therefore belongs to one load, and yours may sit elsewhere on the curve.

Curves compare engines better than a single speedup.

Batching more requests raises total throughput but makes each request slower, so every configuration of an engine is one point on a trade-off between the two. The DeepInfer README plots its benchmarks as Pareto curves, the configurations for which no other configuration gives both more throughput and lower latency, with prefill measured on 4 SM100 GPUs and decode on 64, each within one scale-up domain, a group of GPUs joined by NVIDIA’s fast direct links instead of the slower data-center network. A change that moves the whole curve outward helps at every load. A change that only extends the curve adds a new operating point at one end, which helps only if your product runs there.

“Acceptance” needs a definition.

Claims about speculative decoding often quote an acceptance rate, and the same phrase can mean different things. DeepInfer’s plotting script reads 75% acceptance as 75% of drafted tokens accepted, so five drafts give 1 + 5 × 0.75 = 4.75 tokens per step. Leviathan and colleagues’ 2023 speculative decoding paper instead treats acceptance as the chance that each position is accepted, with the first rejection discarding every later draft, and under that reading the same 75% and five drafts give about 3.3 tokens per step. That is close to the 3.2 to 3.3 accepted tokens DeepSeek reports in production, and well below what the first reading suggests. A claim that depends on acceptance needs to state which definition it uses and to measure the rate on the target workload.

DeepInfer’s sweep script records what ran.

The script that runs DeepInfer’s benchmark sweeps prints the git commit before each sweep, runs each measured point in its own process on its own port, turns off profiling for every measured point, and refuses to plot points whose model, expert-parallel size, context length, draft length or redundant-expert count disagree. Because the command that produces the numbers also produces the record of what ran, the two cannot drift apart.

A negative result belongs in that record too. If a longer draft speeds up a single user but lowers useful throughput at your target concurrency, the finding is the trade and the concurrency where it flips. The same analysis applies to adopting any other DeepInfer mechanism, such as overlap scheduling or expert replication: what resource it saves, what dependency it adds, and the load at which it should help, measured on your workload.

DeepInfer’s benchmark runs with every request present from the start, so it says nothing about queueing under real arrivals. Published results also rarely give the distribution of prompt lengths or cost per useful token at real prices, and equivalence claims for approximate mechanisms are usually argued from averages, which can hide rare failures.
