GLOSSARY.Activation: An intermediate numerical value produced while executing the model.
GLOSSARY.Adapter: A learned modification attached to compatible base weights; LoRA is one family.
GLOSSARY.Autoregressive: Each next-token prediction conditions on earlier tokens.
GLOSSARY.Bandwidth: How many bytes can move per second; distinct from memory capacity.
GLOSSARY.Batch invariance: A supported guarantee that changing co-batch membership does not change a request’s result.
GLOSSARY.BF16 / FP16: Two-byte floating-point formats with different precision/range tradeoffs.
GLOSSARY.Checkpoint: Saved model parameters/configuration at a particular point; may be full weights or only an adapter.
GLOSSARY.Collective: A coordinated communication operation among device ranks, such as all-reduce.
GLOSSARY.CP: Context parallelism: divide sequence work among devices.
GLOSSARY.CUDA graph: A captured device-work graph reused to reduce launch overhead, under shape and memory constraints.
GLOSSARY.Decode: Iteratively extend a sequence using retained model state.
GLOSSARY.DP: Data parallelism: split independent work, with details depending on the layer/system.
GLOSSARY.EPLB: Expert-parallel load balancing: place/map expert work to reduce skew.
GLOSSARY.EP: Expert parallelism: distribute expert ownership across devices.
GLOSSARY.EOS: End-of-sequence marker or corresponding termination condition.
GLOSSARY.FLOP: One floating-point arithmetic operation; FLOP/s measures a rate.
GLOSSARY.GEMM: General matrix multiplication, a central building block of model execution.
GLOSSARY.GQA: Grouped-query attention: query heads share fewer KV heads.
GLOSSARY.HBM: High-bandwidth accelerator memory; capacity and transfer bandwidth are separate limits.
GLOSSARY.Kernel: A device program implementing one or more numerical operations.
GLOSSARY.KV cache: Retained keys and values or compatible attention state for preceding tokens.
GLOSSARY.LoRA: Low-rank adaptation: a compact parameter update to selected base-model matrices.
GLOSSARY.MLA: Multi-head latent attention: compressed attention representations; not a paging scheme.
GLOSSARY.MoE: Mixture of experts: selectively activate expert networks for each token.
GLOSSARY.Oracle: A reference computation or criterion that decides whether a property holds.
GLOSSARY.P99: The value at or below which 99% of measured samples fall; state the sampling boundary.
GLOSSARY.Prefill: Process known input tokens and build attention state.
GLOSSARY.Rank: One participant in a distributed process group.
GLOSSARY.RoPE: Rotary positional embeddings: a positional transformation of attention representations.
GLOSSARY.SLO: Service-level objective: a measurable target such as a latency percentile.
GLOSSARY.Softmax: Convert arbitrary scores to nonnegative probabilities summing to one.
GLOSSARY.SWA: Sliding-window attention: limit directly visible local key positions.
GLOSSARY.Teacher forcing: Feed a known continuation to compare model predictions on identical prefixes.
GLOSSARY.Tensor: A multidimensional array of numerical values.
GLOSSARY.TP: Tensor parallelism: split an operation/tensor across devices.
GLOSSARY.TTFT / ITL: Time to first token / inter-token latency. Specify queueing and delivery boundaries.
GLOSSARY.Weights: Learned numerical parameters defining the model’s calculations.
GLOSSARY.Inference: Running a trained model to make predictions, with its weights held fixed.
GLOSSARY.Inference engine: The software that loads a model’s weights, manages memory, groups requests and runs the calculations that produce each answer.
GLOSSARY.Pareto curve: A plot of the best trade-offs between two goals, here total throughput and per-user speed. Each point on it cannot improve one goal without losing on the other.
GLOSSARY.SM100: NVIDIA’s code name for its Blackwell data-center GPU architecture (for example the B200).
GLOSSARY.FP8 / FP4: Floating-point formats that store a number in 8 or 4 bits. They are usually paired with block scaling so that their very small set of values can cover a useful range.
GLOSSARY.Block scaling: Storing a group of numbers (for example 32) with one shared scale factor, so each stored number only records a small multiple of that scale.
GLOSSARY.Perplexity: The exponential of a model’s average negative log probability per token on some text. Lower means the model found the text less surprising.
GLOSSARY.Tokenizer: The program that splits text into tokens and maps each token to an integer ID, and maps IDs back to text.
GLOSSARY.Token: One piece of text, such as a word, part of a word or a punctuation mark, that the model reads or produces as a single unit.
GLOSSARY.Greedy decoding: Always choosing the highest-scoring next token, with no random draw.
GLOSSARY.Temperature: A number that divides the logits before softmax. Below 1 it concentrates probability on the top tokens, and above 1 it spreads probability out.
GLOSSARY.Top-p / top-k: Sampling filters. Top-k keeps only the k highest-scoring tokens. Top-p keeps the smallest set of top tokens whose probabilities add up to p.
GLOSSARY.Byte-pair encoding: A way to build a tokenizer vocabulary by repeatedly merging the most frequent adjacent pair of symbols in training text.
GLOSSARY.KL divergence: A measure of how different one probability distribution is from another. It is zero when they are identical and infinite when the second distribution gives zero probability to an outcome the first one allows.
GLOSSARY.Attention: The transformer operation in which each position compares its query with other positions’ keys and takes a weighted mix of their values.
GLOSSARY.Query, key, value: Three vectors a layer computes for each position. A query is compared with keys to get attention weights, and the weights decide how much of each value is mixed in.
GLOSSARY.Causal mask: A rule in attention that hides every later position, so a token can only use the tokens before it and itself.
GLOSSARY.Throughput: Total work completed per second across all requests, for example output tokens per second for the whole server.
GLOSSARY.Chunked prefill: Splitting a long prompt into pieces processed over several engine steps, so it fits a per-step token budget.
GLOSSARY.Goodput: The highest request rate at which a chosen share of requests still meets both a time-to-first-token target and a per-token latency target.
GLOSSARY.Quantization: Storing numbers such as weights or cache entries in a narrower format (for example 8 or 4 bits) to save memory and bandwidth, at some cost in precision.
GLOSSARY.Arithmetic intensity: The number of arithmetic operations an operation performs for each byte it moves to or from memory.
GLOSSARY.Ridge point: A device’s peak arithmetic rate divided by its memory bandwidth. Operations with lower arithmetic intensity than this are limited by memory.
GLOSSARY.Roofline model: A bound on an operation’s speed: the lower of the device’s compute peak and its bandwidth times the operation’s arithmetic intensity.
GLOSSARY.MFU: Model FLOPs utilization: the arithmetic a model strictly needs per second, divided by the hardware’s peak arithmetic rate.
GLOSSARY.Batching: Running several requests through the same model step, so that one read of the weights serves all of them.
GLOSSARY.Continuous batching: Batching in which the set of active requests can change between model steps, so a waiting request can take the place of one that finished.
GLOSSARY.Scheduler: The part of an inference engine that decides, before each step, which requests run and how many tokens each one contributes.
GLOSSARY.Preemption: Removing a running request from the batch to free memory, either ending it or recomputing it later from the start.
GLOSSARY.Prefix caching: Keeping the attention state computed for a prompt's beginning so that a later request with the same beginning can skip recomputing it.
GLOSSARY.Copy-on-write: Letting two users share memory until one of them needs to change it, and then copying only the part being changed.
GLOSSARY.MXFP8: An 8-bit floating-point format in which each small group of values shares one scale factor, keeping a wide range at low storage cost.
GLOSSARY.GPUDirect RDMA: An NVIDIA feature that lets a network card read and write GPU memory directly, without staging the data in host memory.
GLOSSARY.RDMA: Remote direct memory access: one machine reads or writes another machine's memory over the network without involving the remote CPU.
GLOSSARY.3FS: Fire-Flyer File System, DeepSeek's open-source distributed file system built on SSDs and RDMA networking.
GLOSSARY.Erasure coding: Storing data as fragments plus extra parity fragments so it survives the loss of some of them. With 10+2 coding, any 2 of the 12 fragments can be lost.
GLOSSARY.Pipeline parallelism: Giving different layers of a model to different devices, so each device runs one stage and passes its activations to the next.
GLOSSARY.NVLink: NVIDIA's direct high-bandwidth link between GPUs, much faster than the network between machines.
GLOSSARY.Scale-up domain: A group of GPUs joined by a fast direct link such as NVLink, so they exchange data much faster than they could over the network.
GLOSSARY.Speculative decoding: Letting a cheap model propose several tokens that the main model checks in one pass, keeping only the tokens the main model accepts.
GLOSSARY.Drafter: The cheap model, or extra model head, that proposes draft tokens in speculative decoding.
GLOSSARY.Target model: The main model in speculative decoding. It checks the drafts, and the final text must follow its output distribution.
GLOSSARY.Disaggregation: Running prefill and decode on separate machines, each with its own scheduling, so the two stages can be scaled independently. The attention state then has to be sent from the prefill machine to the decode machine.
GLOSSARY.Little’s law: For any stable queue, the average number of items inside equals the arrival rate times the average time each item spends there. At 20 requests per second and 6 seconds each, about 120 requests are in the system.
GLOSSARY.Structured output: Generation constrained by a grammar, such as a JSON schema, so that the model can only produce tokens that keep the output valid.
GLOSSARY.Zero-overhead scheduling: DeepInfer’s overlap mode, in which the CPU schedules the next step while the GPU is still running the current one, so outputs are handled one step after they are produced.
GLOSSARY.Probability integral transform: Mapping each sampled value through the cumulative distribution it was supposedly drawn from. If the claim is true, the results are spread evenly between 0 and 1.
GLOSSARY.Kolmogorov–Smirnov test: A statistical test of whether a set of samples follows a given distribution, based on the largest gap between the samples’ cumulative distribution and the expected one.
GLOSSARY.Ascend NPU: Huawei’s AI accelerator chip family. DeepInfer supports the Ascend 950 as its second hardware platform.
GLOSSARY.Chat template: The rule that turns a list of chat messages and roles into the exact text and special tokens a chat-trained model saw during training.
GLOSSARY.Architecture: The arrangement of layers and calculations a model performs, as described by its configuration. Fine-tuning changes the learned numbers inside it but not the arrangement.
GLOSSARY.Artifact manifest: A short record of everything needed to rebuild a model’s computation: base revision, adapter or merged weights, configuration, tokenizer and format, precision and library versions.
GLOSSARY.PEFT: Hugging Face’s library for parameter-efficient fine-tuning, which trains and saves small updates such as LoRA adapters instead of full copies of the weights.
GLOSSARY.Safetensors: A file format that stores named tensors without executable code. Hugging Face models and adapters are usually saved in it.
GLOSSARY.rsLoRA: Rank-stabilized LoRA, a variant that scales the update by lora_alpha / √r instead of lora_alpha / r. The stored matrices look the same, so only the configuration flag says which scale applies.
GLOSSARY.QLoRA: Training LoRA adapters on a base model stored in 4-bit format (NF4). The adapter learns to correct that quantized base.
GLOSSARY.Held-out set: Examples kept out of training and used only for evaluation, so they show how the model behaves beyond the data it was fitted to.
GLOSSARY.Differential testing: Checking one implementation against another implementation of the same specification on the same inputs. It misses bugs in code the two share.
GLOSSARY.Metamorphic test: A test that changes something that should not affect the output, such as which other requests share a batch, and checks that the output stays the same.
GLOSSARY.Coordinated omission: A measurement error in closed-loop benchmarks: when the server stalls, the load generator stops sending, so the delays new requests would have suffered are never recorded.
GLOSSARY.Open-loop benchmark: A load generator that sends requests on its own schedule, independent of how fast the server responds, so that queueing delay appears in the measured latency.
GLOSSARY.Poisson process: A model of random arrivals at a fixed average rate, where each arrival is independent of the others. It is the usual stand-in for traffic from many independent users.

placement.prompt: A model is generating token 501. Why can it reuse the keys and values it computed for the first 500 positions instead of recomputing them?
options: A token's key and value depend only on which token it is, so they are the same in every sentence.
Each position attends only to itself and earlier ones, so later tokens cannot change them.
The weights are frozen during inference, and fixed weights alone make every saved vector permanent.
placement.why: Causal masking means an earlier position never reads later tokens, so its hidden states, keys and values are final once computed. Keys and values do depend on context and position, and frozen weights would not be enough if earlier positions could attend forward.

placement.prompt: Two engines run the same weights with greedy decoding. They agree for 19 tokens and pick different 20th tokens. At that step the reference's top two logits differ by 0.001. What is the most reasonable first reading?
options: One engine's KV cache must be corrupt, since a correct engine reproduces greedy output exactly.
Greedy decoding samples at random among the top tokens, so occasional divergence is expected.
Different arithmetic order can round the logits differently and flip a near tie.
placement.why: Low-precision sums computed in a different order give slightly different results, and a 0.001 gap is within that noise. Greedy decoding is deterministic given the logits, and a cache bug would usually show up as larger logit differences on teacher-forced prefixes.

placement.prompt: On one GPU, a decode step for 32 requests takes far less than 32 times as long as a decode step for one request. What mainly explains this?
options: Each step reads the weights from memory once and applies them to all 32 tokens.
The 32 requests share one KV cache, so attention is computed only once per step.
Only one of the 32 requests produces a token per step, in rotation.
placement.why: Small-batch decoding is limited by moving weights from memory, and a batch spreads that one read over many tokens. Each request still keeps its own KV cache, and every request in the batch gets a token each step.

placement.prompt: A paged KV cache uses pages of 16 token positions. Someone proposes pages of 256 positions. Which trade-off should you expect?
options: Larger pages give more prefix-cache hits because each page covers more shared text.
Less bookkeeping, but more unused slots per last page and coarser prefix sharing.
No memory change, because paging only renames positions and never wastes any slots.
placement.why: A request's final page is usually only partly filled, so bigger pages waste more memory per request, and prefix reuse that works in whole pages can only share complete pages. Fewer, larger pages do reduce metadata and indirection, which is why page size is tuned rather than maximized.

placement.prompt: In an expert-parallel mixture-of-experts layer, a token's router picks experts that live on other GPUs. What has to happen for that token?
options: Every GPU first receives a full copy of the chosen experts' weights for that layer.
Nothing crosses GPUs, because each GPU runs its own tokens through its local experts only.
Its activations go to the GPUs owning those experts, and the outputs come back.
placement.why: Expert parallelism moves tokens to the experts, not weights to the tokens: a dispatch sends activations to the owning ranks and a combine step gathers the weighted results. That exchange is also why one overloaded rank can hold up the rest.

placement.prompt: A team raises the maximum speculative draft length from 3 to 8 tokens. When is that most likely to slow decoding down?
options: When batches are large: extra positions cost compute and later drafts rarely survive.
Never, because the target model checks every draft position in one pass at no extra cost.
Whenever drafts are rejected, because a rejection changes the target model's output distribution.
placement.why: Acceptance compounds, so the sixth to eighth draft positions survive rarely, and once a large batch makes the target compute-bound, verifying them is no longer nearly free. Exact verification keeps the target distribution whatever the acceptance rate, so rejection costs time rather than correctness.

placement.prompt: A LoRA adapter trained on base revision R1 loads onto base revision R2 with no shape errors. What does the clean load establish?
options: That the adapted model behaves as trained, since a LoRA update does not depend on the base values.
Only that names and shapes matched; R2's weight values may not be the ones it was trained on.
Nothing at all, because LoRA loaders skip shape and name checks entirely and accept any file.
placement.why: An adapter is a learned correction to specific base weights, so it is only the trained model on top of those weights. Two revisions of one architecture share shapes but not values, so behavior has to be compared against the trained reference.

placement.prompt: Five repeated runs of the baseline measure 950 to 1,080 tokens/s. A change scores 1,100 tokens/s in a single run. What can you conclude?
options: That the change is a regression, since the baseline sometimes reaches 1,080.
That the change gives about a 10% gain, since it was the only difference.
Not yet; repeat the change as often as the baseline and compare.
placement.why: One run of the change sits just above a baseline that varies by about 13%, so the gain could be noise. Repeating both configurations under the same workload shows whether their ranges actually separate.
